

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: 2.4 GHz radio use
======================================================================

{{Short description|Uses of the  2.4 GHz ISM radio spectrum}}

There are several uses of the 2.4&nbsp;GHz [[ISM radio band]]. Interference may occur between devices operating at [[2.4&nbsp;GHz]]. This article details the different users of the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band, how they cause interference to other users and how they are prone to interference from other users.

==Phone==
{{main|Cordless telephone|Baby monitor}}
Many{{quantify|date=November 2024}} of the [[cordless telephone]]s and [[baby monitor]]s in the [[United States]] and [[Canada]] use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz frequency,<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Gizmodo |title=Why Everything Wireless Is 2.4 GHz |url=https://www.wired.com/2010/09/wireless-explainer/ |access-date=2024-03-12 |magazine=Wired |language=en-US |issn=1059-1028}}</ref> the same frequency at which [[Wi-Fi]] standards [[802.11b]], [[802.11g]], [[802.11n]] and [[802.11ax]] operate.  This can cause a significant decrease in speed, or sometimes{{when|date=November 2024}} the total blocking of the Wi-Fi signal when a conversation on the phone takes place.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wi-Fi Interference – Things That Block Wi-Fi Signal |url=https://www.att.com/internet/wifi-interference-things-that-block-wifi-signals/ |access-date=2024-03-12 |website=AT&T |language=en}}</ref>

==Bluetooth==
{{main|Bluetooth}}
[[Bluetooth]] devices intended for use in short-range [[personal area network]]s operate from 2.4 to 2.4835&nbsp;GHz.  To reduce interference with other protocols that use the 2.45&nbsp;GHz band, the Bluetooth protocol divides the band into 80 channels (numbered from 0 to 79, each 1&nbsp;MHz wide. Bluetooth Low Energy has half the number of channels, with each channel twice as wide as Bluetooth Classic), and changes channels up to 1600 times per second.  Bluetooth also features ''Adaptive Frequency Hopping'' which attempts to detect existing signals in the [[ISM band]], such as [[Wi-Fi]] channels, and avoid them by negotiating a channel map between the communicating Bluetooth devices.

The USB 3.0 computer cable standard has been proven to generate significant amounts of electromagnetic interference that can interfere with any Bluetooth devices a user has connected to the same computer.<ref>{{citation | url = http://www.usb.org/developers/docs/whitepapers/327216.pdf | title = Intel whitepaper "USB 3.0 Radio Frequency Interference on 2.4&nbsp;GHz Devices"}}</ref>

==Wi-Fi==
{{main|Wi-Fi}}
Wi-Fi is technology for radio [[wireless local area network]]ing of devices based on the [[IEEE 802.11]] standards. ''Wi{{nbh}}Fi'' is a trademark of the [[Wi-Fi Alliance]], which restricts the use of the term ''Wi-Fi Certified'' to products that successfully complete [[interoperability]] certification testing.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.webopedia.com/TERM/W/Wi_Fi.html|title=What is Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11x)? A Webopedia Definition|website=Webopedia.com|date=2 May 2001 |url-status=live| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120308123721/http://www.webopedia.com/term/w/wi_fi.html|archive-date=2012-03-08}}</ref>

Devices that can use Wi-Fi technologies include [[desktop computer|desktop]]s and [[laptop]]s, [[video game console]]s, [[smartphone]]s and [[tablet computer|tablet]]s, [[smart TV]]s, digital audio players, cars and modern printers. Wi-Fi compatible devices can connect to the Internet via a WLAN and a [[wireless access point]]. Such an access point (or [[Hotspot (Wi-Fi)|hotspot]]) has a range of about {{convert|20|m|ft|abbr=off|sp=us}} indoors and a greater range outdoors. Hotspot coverage can be as small as a single room with walls that block radio waves, or as large as many square kilometres achieved by using multiple overlapping access points.

Different versions of Wi-Fi exist, with different ranges, radio bands and speeds. Wi-Fi most commonly uses the {{convert|2.4|GHz|cm}} [[UHF]] and {{convert|5.8|GHz|cm|sigfig=1}} [[Super high frequency|SHF]] [[ISM band|ISM]] radio bands; these bands are subdivided into multiple channels. Each channel can be [[Time-division multiple access|time-shared]] by multiple networks. These [[wavelength]]s work best for [[line-of-sight propagation|line-of-sight]]. Many common materials absorb or reflect them, which further restricts range, but can tend to help minimise interference between different networks in crowded environments. At close range, some versions of Wi-Fi, running on suitable hardware, can achieve speeds of over {{nowrap|1 Gbit/s}}.

Anyone within range with a [[wireless network interface controller]] can attempt to access a network; because of this, Wi-Fi is more vulnerable to attack (called [[eavesdropping]]) than wired networks. [[Wi-Fi Protected Access]] (WPA) is a family of technologies created to protect information moving across Wi-Fi networks and includes solutions for personal and enterprise networks. Security features of WPA have included stronger protections and new security practices as the security landscape has changed over time.

To guarantee no interference in any circumstances, the Wi-Fi protocol requires 16.25 (11g/n) or 22&nbsp;MHz (11b) of channel separation (as shown below). Any remaining gap is used as a [[guard band]] to allow sufficient attenuation along the edge channels. This guardband is mainly used to accommodate older routers with modem chipsets prone to full channel occupancy, as most modern Wi-Fi modems are not prone to excessive channel occupancy.

[[Image:2.4 GHz Wi-Fi channels (802.11b,g WLAN).svg|thumb|center|Graphical representation of overlapping 22&nbsp;MHz channels within the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band|599x599px]]

While overlapping frequencies can be configured and will usually work, it can cause interference, resulting in slowdowns, sometimes severe, particularly in heavy use. Certain subsets of frequencies can be used simultaneously at any one location without interference (see diagrams for typical allocations):

[[File:NonOverlappingChannels2.4GHz802.11-en.svg|center|thumb|330px|Graphical representation of Wireless LAN channels in 2.4&nbsp;GHz band. Channels 12 and 13 are customarily unused in North America. As a result, the usual 20&nbsp;MHz allocation becomes 1/6/11, the same as 11b. Note "channel 3" in the 40&nbsp;MHz diagram above is often labelled with the 20&nbsp;MHz channel numbers "1+5" or "1" with "+ Upper" or "5" with "+ Lower" in router interfaces, and "11" as "9+13" or "9" with "+ Upper" or "13" with "+ Lower".]]

However, the exact spacing required when the transmitters are not colocated depends on the protocol, the data rate selected, the distances and the electromagnetic environment where the equipment is used.<ref name="adjacentchannels"/>

{| class="wikitable"
|+Attenuation by channel spacing for 20&nbsp;MHz (OFDM) transmitters<ref name="adjacentchannels"/>{{rp|3}}

|}

The attenuation by relative channel adds to that due to distance and the effects of obstacles. Per the standards, for transmitters on the same channel, transmitters must take turns to transmit if they can detect each other 3&nbsp;dB above the [[noise floor]] (the thermal noise floor is around -101&nbsp;[[dBm]] for 20&nbsp;MHz channels).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.networkcomputing.com/wireless-infrastructure/channel-bonding-wifi-and-radio-frequency-physics|title=Channel Bonding in WiFi and Radio Frequency Physics &#124; Network Computing}}</ref> On the other hand, transmitters will ignore transmitters on other channels if the attenuated signal strength from them is below a threshold P<sub>th</sub> which, for non [[Wi-Fi 6]] systems, is between -76 and -80&nbsp;dBm.<ref name=adjacentchannels/> While there can be interference (bit errors) at a receiver, this is usually small if the received signal is more than 20&nbsp;dB above the attenuated signal strength from transmitters on the other channels.<ref name=adjacentchannels/>

The overall effect is that if there is considerable overlap between adjacent channel transmitters, they will often interfere with each other. In general, using every fourth or fifth channel by leaving three or four channels clear between used channels causes much less interference than sharing channels, and narrower spacing still can be used at further distances.<ref name="compnetworking.about.com">{{cite web |url=https://compnetworking.about.com/od/wifihomenetworking/qt/wifichannel.htm |title=Choosing the right Wi-Fi channel can minimize wireless interference |website=compnetworking.about.com |access-date=5 June 2016 |archive-date=1 July 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160701223751/http://compnetworking.about.com/od/wifihomenetworking/qt/wifichannel.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="adjacentchannels">{{Cite conference |last1=Garcia Villegas |first1=E. |title=Effect of adjacent-channel interference in IEEE 802.11 WLANs |conference=CrownCom 2007 |publisher=ICST & IEEE |year=2007 |url=https://upcommons.upc.edu/e-prints/bitstream/2117/1234/1/CrownCom07_CReady.pdf |display-authors=etal |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720102658/https://upcommons.upc.edu/e-prints/bitstream/2117/1234/1/CrownCom07_CReady.pdf |archive-date=2011-07-20}}</ref>

== Zigbee/IEEE 802.15.4 wireless data networks ==
Many [[Zigbee]]/[[IEEE 802.15.4]]-based wireless data networks operate in the 2.4&ndash;2.4835&nbsp;GHz band, and so are subject to interference from other devices operating in that same band. The definition is for 16 channels numbered 11&ndash;26 to occupy the space, each 2&nbsp;MHz wide and spaced by 5&nbsp;MHz. The F<sub>0</sub> of channel 11 is set at 2.405&nbsp;GHz. The DSSS scheme is used to spread out the spectrum (from a data-rate of 250 kbit/s) and reduce interference.<ref name="nxpbee">{{cite web |title=Co-existence of IEEE 802.15.4 at 2.4&nbsp;GHz Application Note |url=https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/application-note/JN-AN-1079.pdf |website=NXP |date=8 November 2013}}</ref>

To avoid interference from [[IEEE 802.11]] networks, an IEEE 802.15.4 network can be configured to only use channels 15, 20, 25, and 26, avoiding frequencies used by the commonly used [[List of WLAN channels|IEEE 802.11 channels]] 1, 6, and 11. The exact channel selection depends on the local popular 802.11 channel. For example, in a place that uses 1, 7, and 13 channels, the preference would be for channels 15, 16, 21, and 22. Channel coexistence is possible provided 8 meters of spacing between the 802.11 access point and the 802.15.4 device.<ref name="nxpbee"/>

==RF peripherals==
Some wireless peripherals like keyboards and mice use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band with a proprietary protocol.

==Amateur radio==
[[Amateur radio]] operators in the US are able to operate from 2300 to 2450&nbsp;MHz, except for 2310 to 2390&nbsp;MHz. The frequencies between 2400 and 2410&nbsp;MHz are reserved in the United States for amateur satellite communications, and 2410 to 2450&nbsp;MHz for broadband activities. Amateur radio operators are permitted up to 1500 [[watt]]s of power and 22&nbsp;MHz of bandwidth in the 2400&nbsp;MHz band. Various portions of the 2400&nbsp;MHz band are available to amateur radio operators in [[Amateur radio frequency allocations|many other countries]].<ref>{{cite web

==Microwave oven==
{{main|Microwave oven}}
Most domestic [[microwave oven]]s operate by emitting a very high power signal in the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band. Older devices have poor shielding,<ref>{{cite web |date=2021-06-16 |df=dmy-all |title=Microwave ovens and their hazards |department=OSH answers |website=ccohs.ca |series=[[Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety]] |place=Ottawa, CA |publisher=[[Government of Canada]] |url=https://www.ccohs.ca/ |access-date=2021-06-17 }}</ref> and often emit a very "dirty" signal over the entire 2.4&nbsp;GHz band.{{efn|Large industrial or commercial ovens typically use a longer-wave [[ISM radio band|ISM frequency]] near 915&nbsp;MHz.<ref>{{cite web |title=For heat, tune to 915 or 2450&nbsp;Megacycles |year=2007 |publisher=[[Litton Industries]] |orig-date=1965 |via=Southwest Museum of Engineering, Communications, and Computation |url=http://www.smecc.org/litton_-_for_heat,_tune_to_915_or_2450_megacycles.htm |access-date=12 December 2006}}</ref>}}

This can cause considerable difficulties to [[Wi-Fi]] and video<ref>{{cite magazine | last=Arndt | first=Rachel | date=2013-11-21 |df=dmy-all | title=Can the microwave really scramble my WiFi? A handy guide to the electromagnetic interference happening in your home |magazine=[[Popular Mechanics]] | url=https://www.popularmechanics.com/home/how-to/a9768/can-the-microwave-really-scramble-my-wi-fi-16184059/| access-date=6 October 2020}}</ref> transmission, resulting in reduced range or complete blocking of the signal.

The [[IEEE]] [[802.11]] committee that developed the Wi-Fi specification conducted an extensive investigation into the interference potential of microwave ovens. A typical microwave oven uses a self-oscillating [[vacuum tube|vacuum power tube]] called a [[magnetron]] and a high voltage [[power supply]] with a [[Rectifier#Half-wave rectification|half wave rectifier]] (often with [[voltage doubler|voltage doubling]]) and no DC [[Electronic filter|filtering]]. This produces an RF [[pulse train]] with a [[duty cycle]] below 50% as the tube is completely off for half of every [[Mains electricity|AC mains]] cycle: 8.33&nbsp;ms in 60&nbsp;Hz countries and 10&nbsp;ms in 50&nbsp;Hz countries.

This property gave rise to a Wi-Fi microwave oven interference robustness mode that segments larger data frames into fragments, each small enough to fit into the oven's off periods.

The 802.11 committee also found that although the instantaneous frequency of a microwave oven magnetron varies widely over each half AC cycle with the instantaneous supply voltage, at any instant it is relatively [[Coherence (physics)|coherent]], i.e., it occupies only a narrow bandwidth.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Horn | first1 = J. | last2 = Vasudevan | first2 = S. | year = 1997 | title = Modeling and mitigation of interference in the 2.4&nbsp;GHz ISM band | journal = Applied Microwave and Wireless | volume = 9 | pages = 59–71 }}</ref> The [[IEEE 802.11g-2003|802.11a/g]] signal is inherently robust against such interference because it uses [[OFDM]] with [[error correction]] information interleaved across the carriers; as long as only a few carriers are wiped out by strong narrow band interference, the information in them can be regenerated by the error correcting code from the carriers that do get through.

==Audio-visual (AV) devices==
===Baby monitors===
{{main|Baby monitor}}
Some [[baby monitor]]s use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band. Some transmit only audio, but others also provide video.

===Audio devices===
====Wireless microphones====
{{main|Wireless microphone}}
[[Wireless microphone]]s operate as transmitters. Some digital wireless microphones use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band (e.g., AKG model DPT 70).

====Wireless speakers====
{{main|Wireless speaker}}
[[Wireless speaker]]s operate as receivers. The transmitter is a [[preamplifier]] that may be integrated in another device. Some wireless speakers use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band, with a proprietary protocol. They may be subject to dropouts caused by interference from other devices.

===Video devices===
{{main|Video sender}}
[[Video sender]]s typically operate using an [[frequency modulation|FM]] [[Carrier wave|carrier]] to carry a video signal from one room to another (for example, [[satellite TV]] or [[closed-circuit television]]). These devices typically operate continuously but have low (10&nbsp;mW) transmit power. However, some devices, especially wireless cameras, operate with (often unauthorized) high power levels, and have [[high-gain antenna]]s.{{Citation needed|date=July 2009}}

[[Amateur radio]] operators can transmit two-way [[amateur television]] (and voice) in the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band—and all ISM frequencies above 902&nbsp;MHz—with maximum power of 1500&nbsp;watts in the US if the transmission mode does not include [[spread spectrum]] techniques.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.qsl.net/kb9mwr/projects/wireless/pwr.html |title=Part 97 vs Part 15 and Permissible Power Comparison |website=qsl.net |access-date=2016-06-20}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.w5yi.org/page.php?id=142 |title=W5YI : Sec. 97.313 transmitter power standards |website=www.w5yi.org |access-date=2016-06-20}}</ref> Other power levels apply per regions. In the UK, the maximum power level for a full licence is 400&nbsp;watts.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ofcom.org.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0027/62991/amateur-terms.pdf|title=Ofcom amateur terms}}</ref> In other countries, maximum power level for non-spread-spectrum emissions are set by local legislation.{{citation needed|date=September 2015|reason=In the UK the limit is 400W. I think 1500W must be a regional limit (US?) so this should probably be stated}}<!-- UK limit raised in 2024 to 1000W. -->
 
Although the transmitter of some video cameras appears to be fixed on one frequency, it has been found in several models that the cameras are actually frequency agile, and can have their frequency changed by disassembling the product and moving solder links or [[DIP switch]]es inside the camera.

These devices are prone to interference from other 2.4&nbsp;GHz devices, due to the nature of an [[analog video]] signal showing up interference very easily. A carrier-to-noise ratio of some 20&nbsp;dB is required to give a "clean" picture.

Continuous transmissions interfere with these, causing "patterning" on the picture, sometimes a dark or light shift, or complete blocking of the signal.

Non-continuous transmissions, such as Wi-Fi, cause horizontal noise bars to appear on the screen, and can cause "popping" or "clicking" to be heard in the audio.

====Wi-Fi networks====
{{main|Wi-Fi}}
Video senders are a big problem for Wi-Fi networks: Unlike intermittent Wi-Fi, they operate continuously and are typically only 10&nbsp;MHz in bandwidth. This causes a very intense signal as viewed on a spectrum analyser, and completely obliterates over half a channel. The result of this, typically in a [[Wireless Internet service provider]]-type environment, is that clients (who cannot hear the video sender due to the "[[hidden node]]" effect) can hear the Wi-Fi without any issues, but the receiver on the WISP's access point is completely obliterated by the video sender, so is extremely deaf. Furthermore, due to the nature of video senders, they are not interfered with by Wi-Fi easily, since the receiver and transmitter are typically located very close together, so the capture effect is very high. Wi-Fi also has a very wide spectrum, so only typically 30% of the peak power of the Wi-Fi actually affects the video sender. Wi-Fi is not a continuous transmission, so the Wi-Fi signal interferes only intermittently with the video sender. A combination of these factors - low power output of the Wi-Fi compared to the video sender, the fact that typically the video sender is far closer to the receiver than the Wi-Fi transmitter and the FM capture effect means that a video sender may cause problems to Wi-Fi over a wide area, but the Wi-Fi unit causes few problems to the video sender.{{Citation needed|date=July 2009}}

==== Effective isotropic radiated power (EIRP) ====
Many video senders on the market in the UK advertise a 100&nbsp;mW [[equivalent isotropically radiated power]] (EIRP). However, the UK market only permits a 10&nbsp;mW EIRP limit. These devices cause far more interference across a far wider area, due to their excessive power. Furthermore, UK video senders are required to operate across a 20&nbsp;MHz bandwidth (not to be confused with 20&nbsp;MHz [[frequency deviation|deviation]]).

This more widely spread our and stronger power means that some foreign imported video senders are not legal, since they operate on a 15&nbsp;MHz bandwidth or lower, which causes a higher spectral power density, increasing the interference. Furthermore, most other countries permit {{nobr|100 mW EIRP}} for video senders, meaning a lot of video senders in the UK have excessive power outputs.{{citation needed|date=July 2009}}

== Radio control ==
{{main|Radio control}}

===Radio-controlled models===
Many radio-controlled drones, model aircraft, model boats and toys use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band. These radio systems can go up to 500&nbsp;meters in radio-controlled cars and over {{convert|2.5|km}} in drones and airplanes.

=== Garage doors ===
Some garage door openers use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band.

==Car alarm==
{{main|Car alarm}}
Certain car manufacturers use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz frequency for their [[car alarm]] internal movement sensors. These devices transmit on 2.45&nbsp;GHz (between channels 8 and 9) at a strength of 500&nbsp;mW. Because of channel overlap, this will cause problems for channels 6 and 11, which are commonly used default channels for Wi-Fi connections. Because the signal is transmitted as a continuous tone, it causes particular problems for Wi-Fi traffic. This can be clearly seen with spectrum analysers. These devices, due to their short range and high power, are typically not susceptible to interference from other devices on the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band.{{Citation needed|date=August 2011}}

== Radars ==
Some [[radars]] use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band.

== Power ==
===  Smart power meters ===
Some [[Smart meter|'smart' power meters]] use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band.<ref>{{cite web |title=The ARRL Smart Meter FAQ Page |url=https://www.arrl.org/smart-meters |publisher=[[ARRL]]}}</ref>

=== Wireless power ===
Some [[wireless power transmission]] uses the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band.

== USB 3.0 ==
[[USB 3.0]] devices and cables, if not shielded properly, may introduce noise to the 2.4&nbsp;GHz band.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pcmag.com/opinions/wireless-witch-the-truth-about-usb-30-and-wi-fi-interference|title=Wireless Witch: The Truth About USB 3.0 and Wi-Fi Interference|access-date=2023-06-27|website=www.pcmag.com}}</ref>

{{Short description|Uses of radio and radio waves}}
{{Multiple issues|
{{Cleanup reorganize|date=October 2025}}
{{Lead too short|date=October 2025}}
}}

[[Radio]] (the general technology of communicating using radio waves) has many practical applications, which include broadcasting, voice communication, data communication, radar, radiolocation,  medical treatments, and remote control.

== Broadcasting ==
{{further|Broadcasting}}

Broadcasting is the one-way transmission of information from a transmitter to receivers belonging to a public audience.<ref name="Pizzi">{{Cite book |last1=Pizzi |first1=Skip |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DaVwAwAAQBAJ |title=A Broadcast Engineering Tutorial for Non-Engineers, 4th Ed. |last2=Jones |first2=Graham |date=2014 |publisher=National Association of Broadcasters, Taylor and Francis |isbn=978-0415733397 |access-date=2023-03-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154545/https://books.google.com/books?id=DaVwAwAAQBAJ |archive-date=2024-10-03 |url-status=live}}</ref> Since the radio waves become weaker with distance, a [[broadcasting station]] can only be received within a limited distance of its transmitter.<ref name="Witten">{{Cite book |last=Witten |first=Alan Joel |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VzQrDwAAQBAJ&dq=radio+waves+become+weaker+with+distance&pg=PA162 |title=Handbook of Geophysics and Archaeology |publisher=[[Routledge]] |year=2017 |isbn=978-1351564588 |access-date=30 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154550/https://books.google.com/books?id=VzQrDwAAQBAJ&dq=radio+waves+become+weaker+with+distance&pg=PA162#v=onepage&q=radio%20waves%20become%20weaker%20with%20distance&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Systems that broadcast from [[Communication satellite|satellites]] can generally be received over an entire country or continent.  Older terrestrial radio and television are paid for by [[commercial advertising]] or governments.  In subscription systems like satellite television and [[satellite radio]] the customer pays a monthly fee. In these systems, the radio signal is [[encrypted]] and can only be decrypted by the receiver, which is controlled by the company and can be deactivated if the customer does not pay.<ref name="Bonsor-2001">{{Cite web |last=Bonsor |first=Kevin |date=26 September 2001 |title=How Satellite Radio Works |url=https://electronics.howstuffworks.com/satellite-radio.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240328004303/https://electronics.howstuffworks.com/satellite-radio.htm |archive-date=28 March 2024 |access-date=30 August 2022 |website=howstuffworks.com |publisher=HowStuffWorks}}</ref>

Broadcasting uses several parts of the radio spectrum, depending on the type of signals transmitted and the desired target audience. [[Longwave]] and [[medium wave]] signals can give reliable coverage of areas several hundred kilometers across, but have a more limited information-carrying capacity and so work best with audio signals (speech and music), and the sound quality can be degraded by [[radio noise]] from natural and artificial sources.  The [[shortwave]] bands have a greater potential range but are more subject to interference by distant stations and varying atmospheric conditions that affect reception.<ref name="Gosling2">{{Cite book |last=Gosling |first=William |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jqj2k9EXgioC&q=longwave |title=Radio Antennas and Propagation: Radio Engineering Fundamentals |publisher=Newnes |year=1998 |isbn=978-0750637411 |access-date=30 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154546/https://books.google.com/books?id=jqj2k9EXgioC&q=longwave#v=snippet&q=longwave&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Griffin">{{Cite book |last=Griffin |first=B. Whitfield |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m5DIroWLw2EC&q=radio+fundamentals |title=Radio-electronic Transmission Fundamentals |publisher=SciTech Publishing/Noble |year=2000 |isbn=978-1884932137 |access-date=30 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154547/https://books.google.com/books?id=m5DIroWLw2EC&q=radio+fundamentals#v=snippet&q=radio%20fundamentals&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In the [[very high frequency]] band, greater than 30 megahertz, the Earth's atmosphere has less of an effect on the range of signals, and [[line-of-sight propagation]] becomes the principal mode. These higher frequencies permit the great bandwidth required for television broadcasting.  Since natural and artificial noise sources are less present at these frequencies, high-quality audio transmission is possible, using [[frequency modulation]].<ref name="Pizzi-Jones">{{Cite book |last1=Pizzi |first1=Skip |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sQ1xAwAAQBAJ&dq=vhf+propagation+television&pg=PR9 |title=A Broadcast Engineering Tutorial for Non-Engineers |last2=Jones |first2=Graham |publisher=CRC Press/Focal Press |year=2014 |isbn=978-1317906834 |access-date=30 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154549/https://books.google.com/books?id=sQ1xAwAAQBAJ&dq=vhf+propagation+television&pg=PR9#v=onepage&q=vhf%20propagation%20television&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Perez">{{Cite book |last=Perez |first=Reinaldo |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dPBGBQAAQBAJ&dq=vhf+uhf+noise&pg=PA756 |title=Handbook of Electromagnetic Compatibility |publisher=Academic Press |year=2013 |isbn=978-1483288970 |access-date=30 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154548/https://books.google.com/books?id=dPBGBQAAQBAJ&dq=vhf+uhf+noise&pg=PA756#v=onepage&q=vhf%20uhf%20noise&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Audio: Radio broadcasting ===
{{main|Radio broadcasting}}

[[Radio broadcasting]] means transmission of [[Audio signal|audio]] (sound) to [[radio receiver]]s belonging to a public audience.  Analog audio is the earliest form of radio broadcast. [[AM broadcasting]] began around 1920. [[FM broadcasting]] was introduced in the late 1930s with improved [[fidelity]].  A broadcast radio receiver is called a ''radio''.  Most radios can receive both AM and FM.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Green |first1=Clarence R. |title=The Theory and Servicing of AM, FM, and FM Stereo Receivers |last2=Bourque |first2=Robert M. |publisher=Prentice-Hall |year=1980 |page=6}}</ref>

| width3            = 266
| footer            = 
}}

* AM ([[amplitude modulation]]) – in AM, the [[amplitude]] (strength) of the radio carrier wave is varied by the audio signal. [[AM broadcasting]], the oldest broadcasting technology, is allowed in the [[AM broadcast band|AM broadcast bands]], between 148 and 283&nbsp;kHz in the [[low frequency]] (LF) band for longwave broadcasts and between 526 and 1706&nbsp;kHz in the [[medium frequency]] (MF) band for medium-wave broadcasts.<ref>{{Cite report |title=Radio – Preparing for the Future |date=October 2005 |publisher=[[Ofcom]] |place=London |page=2 |access-date=2022-09-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911114834/https://www.ofcom.org.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0020/33392/appendix_c.pdf |archive-date=2022-09-11 |url-status=live |section-url=https://www.ofcom.org.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0020/33392/appendix_c.pdf |section=Appendix&nbsp;C: Glossary}}</ref> Because waves in these bands travel as [[Ground wave|ground waves]] following the terrain, [[AM station|AM radio stations]] can be received beyond the horizon at hundreds of miles distance, but AM has lower fidelity than FM. Radiated power ([[Effective radiated power|ERP]]) of AM stations in the US is usually limited to a maximum of 10&nbsp;kW, although a few ([[clear-channel stations]]) are allowed to transmit at 50&nbsp;kW. AM stations broadcast in monaural audio; [[AM stereo]] broadcast standards exist in most countries, but the radio industry has failed to upgrade to them, due to lack of demand.<ref name="Gupta-2021">{{Cite book |last=Gupta |first=Rakesh |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KjgvEAAAQBAJ&dq=am+mode+broadcasting&pg=PA84 |title=Education Technology in Physical Education and Sports |publisher=Friends Publications |year=2021 |isbn=978-9390649808 |series=Audio Visual Media in Physical Education |location=India |access-date=30 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003154550/https://books.google.com/books?id=KjgvEAAAQBAJ&dq=am+mode+broadcasting&pg=PA84#v=onepage&q=am%20mode%20broadcasting&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

:* [[Shortwave listening|Shortwave broadcasting]] – AM broadcasting is also allowed in the [[shortwave]] bands by legacy radio stations at 3 – 30 MHz. Since radio waves in these bands can travel intercontinental distances by reflecting off the [[ionosphere]] using [[skywave]] or "skip" propagation, shortwave is used by international stations, broadcasting to other countries.<ref name="Gupta-2021" /><ref name="Berg-2008">{{Cite book |last=Berg |first=Jerome S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ux9fZj6izuEC&dq=DRM+broadcasting&pg=PA51 |title=Broadcasting on the Short Waves: 1945 to today |publisher=McFarland |year=2008 |isbn=978-0786451982 |access-date=30 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155140/https://books.google.com/books?id=Ux9fZj6izuEC&dq=DRM+broadcasting&pg=PA51#v=onepage&q=DRM%20broadcasting&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

| direction         = horizontal

* FM ([[frequency modulation]]) – in FM the [[frequency]] of the radio carrier signal is varied slightly by the audio signal. [[FM broadcasting]] is permitted in the [[FM broadcast band|FM broadcast bands]] between about 65 and 108&nbsp;MHz in the [[very high frequency]] (VHF) range. Radio waves in this band travel by [[Line-of-sight propagation|line-of-sight]] so FM reception is limited by the visual [[horizon]] to about {{convert|30-40|miles|km|abbr=on|sigfig=2}}, and can be blocked by hills. However it is less susceptible to interference from [[radio noise]] ([[Radio frequency interference|RFI]], [[sferics]], static), and has higher [[fidelity]], better [[frequency response]], and less [[audio distortion]] than AM. In the US, radiated power ([[Effective radiated power|ERP]]) of FM stations varies from 6–100&nbsp;kW.<ref name="Sterling-Kieth">{{Cite book |last1=Sterling |first1=Christopher H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ik-3w8ZwwqkC&q=propagation |title=Sounds of Change: A history of FM broadcasting in America |last2=Kieth |first2=Michael C. |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0807877555 |access-date=30 August 2022}}</ref>
* [[Digital radio]] involves a variety of standards and technologies for broadcasting digital radio signals over the air. Some systems, such as [[HD Radio]] and [[Digital Radio Mondiale|DRM]], operate in the same wavebands as analog broadcasts, either as a replacement for analog stations or as a complementary service. Others, such as [[Digital Audio Broadcasting|DAB/DAB+]] and [[ISDB]]_Tsb, operate in wavebands traditionally used for television or satellite services.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://tech.ebu.ch/docs/digitalradio/WBU%20Radio%20Techologies%20Guide.pdf |title=Digital Radio Guide |year=2017 |publisher=World Broadcasting Unions |place=Switzerland |access-date=2022-08-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230406214022/https://tech.ebu.ch/docs/digitalradio/WBU%20Radio%20Techologies%20Guide.pdf |archive-date=2023-04-06 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Portable_radio_receiving_DAB+_transmission_in_UK.jpg|thumb|"Roberts" radio for DAB]]

:* [[Digital Audio Broadcasting]] (DAB) debuted in some countries in 1998. It transmits audio as a [[digital signal]] rather than an [[analog signal]] as AM and FM do.<ref name="Baker">{{Cite magazine |last=Baker |first=William |date=2020 |title=DAB vs. FM: The differences between analog and digital radio |url=https://radiofidelity.com/dab-vs-fm-radio/ |access-date=14 September 2020 |magazine=Radio Fidelity online magazine}}</ref> DAB has the potential to provide higher quality sound than FM (although many stations do not choose to transmit at such high quality), has greater immunity to [[radio noise]] and interference, makes better use of scarce [[radio spectrum]] bandwidth and provides advanced user features such as [[electronic program guide]]s. Its disadvantage is that it is incompatible with previous radios so that a new DAB receiver must be purchased.<ref name="Hoeg-Lauterbach">{{Cite book |last1=Hoeg |first1=Wolfgang |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xp8Cd8NxhBUC&q=DAB+broadcasting |title=Digital Audio Broadcasting: Principles and applications of digital radio |last2=Lauterbach |first2=Thomas |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=2004 |isbn=978-0470871423 |access-date=30 August 2022}}</ref> Several nations have set dates to switch off analog FM networks in favor of DAB / DAB+, notably Norway in 2017<ref>{{Cite news |last=Revel |first=Timothy |date=10 January 2017 |title=Norway is first country to turn off FM radio and go digital-only |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2117569-norway-is-first-country-to-turn-off-fm-radio-and-go-digital-only/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170127121228/https://www.newscientist.com/article/2117569-norway-is-first-country-to-turn-off-fm-radio-and-go-digital-only/ |archive-date=27 January 2017 |access-date=4 September 2022 |work=[[New Scientist]] |language=en-US}}</ref> and Switzerland in 2024.<ref>{{Cite news |last=McLane |first=Paul |date=30 August 2021 |title=Swiss FM shutdown reverts to original 2024 date |url=https://www.radioworld.com/global/swiss-fm-shutdown-reverts-to-original-2024-date |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221023165018/https://www.radioworld.com/global/swiss-fm-shutdown-reverts-to-original-2024-date |archive-date=23 October 2022 |access-date=4 September 2022 |work=Radio World |language=en-US}}</ref>

:: A single DAB station transmits a {{frequency|1,500|kHz}} bandwidth signal that carries from 9–12&nbsp;channels of digital audio modulated by [[OFDM]] from which the listener can choose. Broadcasters can transmit a channel at a range of different [[bit rates]], so different channels can have different audio quality.  In different countries DAB stations broadcast in either [[Band III]] (174–240&nbsp;MHz) or [[L band]] (1.452–1.492&nbsp;GHz) in the UHF range, so like FM reception is limited by the visual horizon to about {{convert|40|miles|km|sigfig=2}}.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Trends in Radio Research: Diversity, innovation, and policies |publisher=Cambridge Scholars Publishing |year=2018 |page=263}}</ref><ref name="Hoeg-Lauterbach" />

:* [[HD Radio]] is an alternative digital radio standard widely implemented in North America.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://news.wjct.org/news/2017-11-27/the-state-of-hd-radio-in-jacksonville-and-nationwide |title=The state of HD&nbsp;Radio in Jacksonville and nationwide |last=Bortzfield |first=Bill |date=27 November 2017 |access-date=4 September 2022 |lang=en |website=[[WJCT]] Public Media}}</ref> An [[in-band on-channel]] technology, HD&nbsp;Radio broadcasts a digital signal in a subcarrier of a station's analog FM or AM signal. Stations are able to [[multicast]] more than one audio signal in the subcarrier, supporting the transmission of multiple audio services at varying bitrates.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://www.rbr.com/mib0816/ |title=Transmitter & programming considerations for HD&nbsp;Radio |last=Hadfield |first=Marty |date=15 August 2016 |access-date=4 September 2022 |website=RBR + TVBR (rbr.com)}}</ref> The digital signal is transmitted using [[OFDM]] with the HDC ([[High-Definition Coding]]) proprietary [[audio compression format]]. HDC is based on, but not compatible with, the [[MPEG-4]] standard [[HE-AAC]].<ref>{{Cite web |author1=Theori |date=9 June 2017 |title=Receiving NRSC‑5 |url=http://theori.io/research/nrsc-5-c |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170820185827/http://theori.io/research/nrsc-5-c |archive-date=20 August 2017 |access-date=14 April 2018 |website=theori.io}}</ref> It uses a [[modified discrete cosine transform]] (MDCT) [[audio data compression]] algorithm.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Jones |first1=Graham A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=K9N1TVhf82YC&pg=PA558 |title=NAB Engineering Handbook |last2=Layer |first2=David H. |last3=Osenkowsky |first3=Thomas G. |publisher=[[National Association of Broadcasters]] / [[Taylor & Francis]] |year=2013 |isbn=978-1136034107 |pages=558–559}}</ref>

:* [[Digital Radio Mondiale]] (DRM) is a competing digital terrestrial radio standard developed mainly by broadcasters as a higher [[spectral efficiency]] replacement for legacy AM and FM broadcasting. ''Mondiale'' means "worldwide" in French and Italian; DRM was developed in 2001, and is currently supported by 23&nbsp;countries, and adopted by some European and Eastern broadcasters beginning in 2003. The ''DRM30'' mode uses the commercial broadcast bands below 30&nbsp;MHz, and is intended as a replacement for standard AM broadcast on the [[Longwave#longwave broadcasting anchor|longwave]], [[AM broadcasting|mediumwave]], and [[Shortwave radio#shortwave broadcasting anchor|shortwave]] bands. The ''DRM+'' mode uses [[VHF]] frequencies centered around the FM broadcast band, and is intended as a replacement for FM broadcasting. It is incompatible with existing radio receivers, so it requires listeners to purchase a new DRM receiver. The modulation used is a form of [[OFDM]] called [[COFDM]] in which, up to 4&nbsp;carriers are transmitted on a channel formerly occupied by a single AM or FM signal, modulated by [[quadrature amplitude modulation]] (QAM).<ref name="ETSI-201-980">{{Cite report |url=https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_es/201900_201999/201980/04.02.01_60/es_201980v040201p.pdf |title=DRM System Specification |date=January 2021 |publisher=European Broadcasting Union |place=Geneva, CH |page=178 |id=ETSI ES 201 980 |access-date=19 April 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210118162612/https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_es/201900_201999/201980/04.02.01_60/es_201980v040201p.pdf |archive-date=18 January 2021 |via=ETSI.org |url-status=live |type=vers.&nbsp;4.2.1}}</ref><ref name="Berg-2008" />
:: The DRM system is designed to be as compatible as possible with existing AM and FM radio transmitters, so that much of the equipment in existing radio stations can continue in use, augmented with DRM modulation equipment.<ref name="ETSI-201-980" /><ref name="Berg-2008" />

[[File:SiriusXM_Display_on_Volkswagen's_RNS-510_Receiver.png|thumb|Volkswagen's RNS-510 receiver supports [[Sirius Satellite Radio]].]]

* [[Satellite radio]] is a subscription radio service that broadcasts CD quality [[digital audio]] direct to subscribers' receivers using a [[microwave]] [[downlink]] signal from a [[Communications satellite|direct broadcast communication satellite]] in [[geostationary]] orbit {{convert|22,000|miles}} above the Earth. It is mostly intended for [[Car radio|radios in vehicles]]. Satellite radio uses the 2.3&nbsp;GHz [[S band]] in North America, in other parts of the world, it uses the 1.4&nbsp;GHz {{nobr|[[L band]]}} allocated for DAB.<ref name="Satellite S-2011">{{Cite report |url=http://www.csgnetwork.com/satradiofreq.html |title=Satellite S‑band radio frequency table |date=15 August 2011 |access-date=23 April 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225175235/http://www.csgnetwork.com/satradiofreq.html |archive-date=25 February 2021 |via=CSG Network |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="kbonsor">{{Cite web |last=Bonsor |first=Kevin |date=26 September 2001 |title=How satellite radio works |url=http://electronics.howstuffworks.com/satellite-radio.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160126111436/http://electronics.howstuffworks.com/satellite-radio.htm |archive-date=26 January 2016 |access-date=1 May 2013 |website=[[HowStuffWorks]]}}</ref>

=== Industrial, scientific, medical ===
The [[ISM bands]] were initially reserved for non-communications uses of RF energy, such as [[microwave ovens]], radio-frequency heating, and similar purposes. However, in recent years the largest use of these bands has been by short-range low-power communications systems, since users do not have to hold a radio operator's license. [[Cordless telephones]], [[Wi-Fi|wireless computer networks]], [[Bluetooth]] devices, and [[Garage door opener|garage door openers]] all use the ISM bands. ISM devices do not have regulatory protection against interference from other users of the band.

=== Audio/video: Television broadcasting ===
{{main|Television broadcasting}}

[[Television broadcasting]] is the transmission of moving images along with a synchronized audio (sound) channel by radio. The sequence of still images is displayed on a screen on a [[television receiver]] (a "television" or TV), which includes a [[loudspeaker]]. Television ([[video]]) signals occupy a wider [[Bandwidth (signal processing)|bandwidth]] than broadcast radio ([[Audio signal|audio]]) signals.  [[Analog television]], the original television technology, required 6&nbsp;MHz, so the television frequency bands are divided into 6&nbsp;MHz channels, now called "RF channels".<ref name="Enticknap">{{Cite book |last=Enticknap |first=Leo Douglas Graham |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ghnGAwholkcC&dq=Television+broadcasting+is+the+transmission+of+moving+images+by+radio%2C&pg=PA163 |title=Moving Image Technology: From Zoetrope to Digital |publisher=Wallflower Press ([[Columbia University Press]]) |year=2005 |isbn=978-1904764069 |access-date=31 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155154/https://books.google.com/books?id=ghnGAwholkcC&dq=Television+broadcasting+is+the+transmission+of+moving+images+by+radio%2C&pg=PA163#v=onepage&q=Television%20broadcasting%20is%20the%20transmission%20of%20moving%20images%20by%20radio%2C&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Designations for television and FM radio broadcast frequencies vary between countries, see [[Television channel frequencies]] and [[FM broadcast band]]. Since VHF and UHF frequencies are desirable for many uses in urban areas, in North America some parts of the former television broadcasting band have been reassigned to [[cellular phone]] and various land mobile communications systems. Even within the allocation still dedicated to television, [[TV-band device|TV-band devices]] use channels without local broadcasters.

The [[Apex (radio band)|Apex]] band in the United States was a pre-WWII allocation for VHF audio broadcasting; it was made obsolete after the introduction of FM broadcasting.

The current television standard, introduced beginning in 1998, is a digital format called [[high-definition television]] (HDTV), which transmits pictures at higher resolution, typically 1080 [[pixels]] high by 1920 pixels wide, at a rate of 50 or 60 interlaced fields/progressive frames per second. [[Digital television]] (DTV) transmission systems, which replaced older analog television in a [[Digital television transition|transition]] beginning in 2006, use [[image compression]] and high-efficiency digital modulation such as [[OFDM]] and [[8VSB]] to transmit HDTV video within a smaller bandwidth than the old analog channels, saving scarce [[radio spectrum]] space.  Therefore, each of the 6&nbsp;MHz analog RF channels now carries up to 7 DTV channels – these are called "virtual channels". Digital television receivers have different behavior in the presence of poor reception or noise than analog television, called the "[[digital cliff]]" effect.  Unlike analog television, in which increasingly poor reception causes the picture quality to gradually degrade, in digital television picture quality is not affected by poor reception until, at a certain point, the receiver stops working and the screen goes black.<ref name="Starks">{{Cite book |last=Starks |first=M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DLssmgEACAAJ |title=The Digital Television Revolution: Origins to Outcomes |publisher=Springer |year=2013 |isbn=978-1137273345 |access-date=31 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155141/https://books.google.com/books?id=DLssmgEACAAJ |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Brice">{{Cite book |last=Brice |first=Richard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Tm_U-Qd58RgC&dq=digital+tv+digital+cliff&pg=PA81 |title=Newnes Guide to Digital TV |publisher=Newnes |year=2002 |isbn=978-0750657211 |access-date=31 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155142/https://books.google.com/books?id=Tm_U-Qd58RgC&dq=digital+tv+digital+cliff&pg=PA81#v=onepage&q=digital%20tv%20digital%20cliff&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

* [[Terrestrial television]], ''over-the-air (OTA) television'', or ''broadcast television'' – the oldest television technology, is the transmission of television signals from land-based television stations to [[Television receiver|television receivers]] (called ''televisions'' or TVs) in viewer's homes.  Terrestrial television broadcasting uses the bands 41 – 88&nbsp;MHz ([[VHF]] low band or [[Band I]], carrying RF channels 1–6), 174 – 240&nbsp;MHz, (VHF high band or [[Band III]]; carrying RF channels 7–13), and 470 – 614&nbsp;MHz ([[UHF]] [[Band IV]] and [[Band V]]; carrying RF channels 14 and up).<ref name="NAB1">{{Cite book |last=Bartlet |first=George W. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eRquswEACAAJ |title=NAB Engineering Handbook, 6th Ed. |date=1975 |publisher=National Association of Broadcasters |location=Washington, D.C. |page=21 |access-date=2023-03-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155143/https://books.google.com/books?id=eRquswEACAAJ |archive-date=2024-10-03 |url-status=live}}</ref>  The exact frequency boundaries vary in different countries.<ref name="Lundstrom">{{Cite book |last=Lundstrom |first=Lars-Ingemar |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=upjcAwAAQBAJ&dq=television+channel+frequencies+europe&pg=PA290 |title=Understanding Digital Television: An Introduction to DVB Systems with Satellite, Cable, Broadband and Terrestrial TV Distribution |publisher=CRC Press |year=2012 |isbn=978-1136032820 |access-date=2022-09-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155143/https://books.google.com/books?id=upjcAwAAQBAJ&dq=television+channel+frequencies+europe&pg=PA290#v=onepage&q=television%20channel%20frequencies%20europe&f=false |archive-date=2024-10-03 |url-status=live}}</ref>  Propagation is by [[Line-of-sight propagation|line-of-sight]], so reception is limited by the visual horizon.<ref name="Ingram">{{Cite book |last=Ingram |first=Dave |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QbcZTrYhheoC&q=television+propagation+line+of+sight+rabbit+ears |title=Video Electronics Technology |publisher=TAB Books |year=1983 |isbn=978-0830614745 |access-date=1 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155246/https://books.google.com/books?id=QbcZTrYhheoC&q=television+propagation+line+of+sight+rabbit+ears |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>  In the US, the [[effective radiated power]] (ERP) of television transmitters is regulated according to [[height above average terrain]].<ref name="ProStar">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=25usF6PafMcC&dq=television+tramsitter+ERP+limits&pg=PA70 |title=Federal Communications Commission (Parts 20 - 39) |publisher=ProStar Publications |isbn=9781577858461 |access-date=2022-09-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155144/https://books.google.com/books?id=25usF6PafMcC&dq=television+tramsitter+ERP+limits&pg=PA70#v=onepage&q=television%20tramsitter%20ERP%20limits&f=false |archive-date=2024-10-03 |url-status=live}}</ref> Viewers closer to the television transmitter can use a simple "rabbit ears" [[dipole antenna]] on top of the TV, but viewers in [[fringe reception]] areas typically require an outdoor antenna mounted on the roof to get adequate reception.<ref name="Ingram" />

* Satellite television – a [[set-top box]] which receives subscription [[direct-broadcast satellite television]], and displays it on an ordinary television. A [[direct broadcast satellite]] in [[geostationary]] orbit {{convert|22200|mi|km|sigfig=3}} above the Earth's [[equator]] transmits many channels (up to 900) modulated on a 12.2 to 12.7&nbsp;GHz [[Ku band|K<sub>u</sub> band]] [[microwave]] downlink signal to a rooftop [[satellite dish]] antenna on the subscriber's residence.  The microwave signal is converted to a lower [[intermediate frequency]] at the dish and conducted into the building by a coaxial cable to a [[set-top box]] connected to the subscriber's TV, where it is demodulated and displayed. The subscriber pays a monthly fee.<ref name="Benoit">{{Cite book |last=Benoit |first=Herve |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4MLy2qXARXYC&q=Satellite+television |title=Satellite Television: Analogue and Digital Reception Techniques |publisher=Butterworth-Heinemann/Arnold |year=1999 |isbn=978-0340741085 |access-date=1 September 2022}}</ref><ref name="Long">{{Cite book |last=Long |first=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L4yQ0iztvQEC&q=Satellite+television |title=The Digital Satellite TV Handbook |publisher=Newnes |year=1999 |isbn=978-0750671712 |access-date=1 September 2022}}</ref>

=== Time and frequency ===
Government [[Standard frequency and time signal service|standard frequency and time signal services]] operate time radio stations which continuously broadcast extremely accurate time signals produced by [[atomic clocks]], as a reference to synchronize other clocks.<ref name="Weik">{{Cite book |last=Weik |first=Martin H. |title=Computer Science and Communications Dictionary |publisher=Computer Science and Communications Dictionary. Springer |year=2000 |isbn=978-0792384250 |page=1649 |chapter=standard frequency and time signal |doi=10.1007/1-4020-0613-6_18062 |access-date=1 September 2022 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/referenceworkentry/10.1007/1-4020-0613-6_18062 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220901212811/https://link.springer.com/referenceworkentry/10.1007/1-4020-0613-6_18062 |archive-date=1 September 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>  Examples are [[BPC (time signal)|BPC]], [[DCF77]], [[JJY]], [[Time from NPL (MSF)|MSF]], [[RTZ (radio station)|RTZ]], [[TDF time signal|TDF]], [[WWV (radio station)|WWV]], and [[YVTO]].<ref name="RadioNavAids">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cU9k_GDAzDAC&q=Radio+Aids+to+Navigation%2C+Publication+117 |title=Radio Aids to Navigation, Publication 117, Chapter 2, Radio Time Signals |publisher=Lighthouse Press |year=2005 |isbn=978-1577855361 |access-date=1 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155702/https://books.google.com/books?id=cU9k_GDAzDAC&q=Radio+Aids+to+Navigation%2C+Publication+117#v=snippet&q=Radio%20Aids%20to%20Navigation%2C%20Publication%20117&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>  One use is in [[radio clocks]] and watches, which include an automated receiver that periodically (usually weekly) receives and decodes the time signal and resets the watch's internal [[quartz clock]] to the correct time, thus allowing a small watch or desk clock to have the same accuracy as an atomic clock.  Government time stations are declining in number because [[GPS]] satellites and the Internet [[Network Time Protocol]] (NTP) provide equally accurate time standards.<ref name="NPR">{{Cite web |date=25 August 2018 |title=What Closing A Government Radio Station Would Mean For Your Clocks |url=https://www.npr.org/2018/08/25/641835302/what-closing-a-government-radio-station-would-mean-for-your-clocks |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201125161858/https://www.npr.org/2018/08/25/641835302/what-closing-a-government-radio-station-would-mean-for-your-clocks |archive-date=25 November 2020 |access-date=1 September 2022 |work=NPR |publisher=National Public Radio, Weekend Edition}}</ref>

=== Citizens' band and personal radio services ===
[[Citizens' band radio]] is allocated in many countries, using channelized radios in the upper HF part of the spectrum (around 27&nbsp;MHz). It is used for personal, small business and hobby purposes. Other frequency allocations are used for similar services in different jurisdictions, for example [[UHF CB]] is allocated in Australia. A wide range of [[Personal radio service|personal radio services]] exist around the world, usually emphasizing short-range communication between individuals or for small businesses, simplified license requirements or in some countries covered by a class license, and usually FM transceivers using around 1 watt or less.

== Voice communication ==

=== Two-way voice communication ===
{{main|Two-way radio}}

{{multiple image

A [[two-way radio]] is an [[Audio signal|audio]] [[transceiver]], a [[Radio receiver|receiver]] and [[transmitter]] in the same device, used for bidirectional person-to-person voice communication with other users with similar radios. An older term for this mode of communication is ''[[radiotelephony]]''.  The radio link may be [[half-duplex]], as in a [[walkie-talkie]], using a single radio channel in which only one radio can transmit at a time, so different users take turns talking, pressing a "[[push to talk]]" button on their radio which switches off the receiver and switches on the transmitter.  Or the radio link may be [[full duplex]], a bidirectional link using two radio channels so both people can talk at the same time, as in a cell phone.<ref name="Frenzel">{{Cite book |last=Frenzel |first=Louis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uqjRDgAAQBAJ&dq=two+way+radio+duplex&pg=PA161 |title=Electronics Explained: Fundamentals for Engineers, Technicians, and Makers |publisher=Newnes |year=2017 |isbn=978-0128118795 |access-date=2 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155805/https://books.google.com/books?id=uqjRDgAAQBAJ&dq=two+way+radio+duplex&pg=PA161#v=onepage&q=two%20way%20radio%20duplex&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

* [[Cell phone]] – a portable wireless telephone that is connected to the [[Public switched telephone network|telephone network]] by radio signals exchanged with a local antenna at a [[cellular base station]] ([[cell tower]]).<ref name="HowCellPhonesWork">{{Cite web |last1=Brain |first1=Marshall |last2=Tyson |first2=Jeff |last3=Layton |first3=Julia |date=2018 |title=How Cell Phones Work |url=https://electronics.howstuffworks.com/cell-phone.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181231064102/https://electronics.howstuffworks.com/cell-phone.htm |archive-date=31 December 2018 |access-date=31 December 2018 |website=How Stuff Works |publisher=InfoSpace Holdings LLC}}</ref> The service area covered by the provider is divided into small geographical areas called "cells", each served by a separate base station antenna and multichannel [[transceiver]].  All the cell phones in a cell communicate with this antenna on separate frequency channels, assigned from a common pool of frequencies. The purpose of cellular organization is to conserve radio bandwidth by [[frequency reuse]].  Low power transmitters are used so the radio waves used in a cell do not travel far beyond the cell, allowing the same frequencies to be reused in geographically separated cells.  When a user carrying a cellphone crosses from one cell to another, his phone is automatically "handed off" seamlessly to the new antenna and assigned new frequencies.  Cellphones have a highly automated [[full duplex]] digital [[transceiver]] using [[OFDM]] modulation using two digital radio channels, each carrying one direction of the bidirectional conversation, as well as a control channel that handles dialing calls and "handing off" the phone to another cell tower.  Older [[2G]], [[3G]], and [[4G]] networks use frequencies in the [[UHF]] and low microwave range, between 700&nbsp;MHz and 3&nbsp;GHz.  The cell phone transmitter adjusts its power output to use the minimum power necessary to communicate with the cell tower; 0.6&nbsp;W when near the tower, up to 3&nbsp;W when farther away.  Cell tower channel transmitter power is 50&nbsp;W.  Current generation phones, called [[smartphones]], have many functions besides making telephone calls, and therefore have several other radio transmitters and receivers that connect them with other networks: usually a [[Wireless modem|Wi-Fi modem]], a [[Bluetooth]] modem, and a [[GPS receiver]].<ref name="Lawson">{{Cite web |last=Lawson |first=Stephen |title=Ten Ways Your Smartphone Knows Where You Are |url=https://www.pcworld.com/article/469718/ten_ways_your_smartphone_knows_where_you_are.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220902190138/https://www.pcworld.com/article/469718/ten_ways_your_smartphone_knows_where_you_are.html |archive-date=2 September 2022 |access-date=2 September 2022 |publisher=[[PCWorld]]}}</ref><ref name="Zander">{{Cite book |last1=Guowang Miao |author-link=Guowang Miao |title=Fundamentals of Mobile Data Networks |last2=Jens Zander |last3=Ki Won Sung |last4=Ben Slimane |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=2016 |isbn=978-1107143210}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=1 January 2006 |title=Cellular Telephone Basics |url=http://www.privateline.com/Cellbasics/Cellbasics02.html |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120417220750/http://www.privateline.com/Cellbasics/Cellbasics02.html |archive-date=17 April 2012 |access-date=2 September 2022 |publisher=Privateline.com |page=2}}</ref>

{{multiple image
| align             = left
| direction         = horizontal

* [[5G|5G cellular network]] – next-generation cellular networks which began deployment in 2019.  Their major advantage is much higher [[data rates]] than previous cellular networks, up to 10&nbsp;[[Bits per second|Gbps]]; 100 times faster than the previous cellular technology, [[4G LTE]]. The higher data rates are achieved partly by using higher frequency radio waves, in the higher microwave band 3–6&nbsp;GHz, and [[millimeter wave]] band, around 28 and 39&nbsp;GHz.  Since these frequencies have a shorter range than previous cellphone bands, the cells will be smaller than the cells in previous cellular networks which could be many miles across.  Millimeter-wave cells will only be a few blocks long, and instead of a [[Cell site|cell base station]] and antenna tower, they will have many small antennas attached to utility poles and buildings.<ref name="S.Brown">{{Cite web |last=Brown |first=Sara |date=13 February 2020 |title=5G, explained |url=https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/5g-explained |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155704/https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/5g-explained |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=2 September 2022 |website=mitsloan.mit.edu |publisher=MIT Sloan School of Management}}</ref><ref name="Osseiran-Monserrat-Marsch">{{Cite book |last1=Osseiran |first1=Afif |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qnMjDAAAQBAJ&q=5G+explained |title=5G Mobile and Wireless Communications Technology |last2=Monserrat |first2=Jose F. |last3=Marsch |first3=Patrick |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2016 |isbn=978-1107130098 |access-date=2 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155705/https://books.google.com/books?id=qnMjDAAAQBAJ&q=5G+explained#v=snippet&q=5G%20explained&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Zivile_Satellitentelefone.jpg|thumb|Satellite phones, showing the large antennas needed to communicate with the satellite]]

* [[Satellite phone]] (''satphone'') – a portable wireless telephone similar to a cell phone, connected to the [[Public switched telephone network|telephone network]] through a radio link to an orbiting [[communications satellite]] instead of through [[cell towers]].  They are more expensive than cell phones; but their advantage is that, unlike a cell phone which is limited to areas covered by cell towers, satphones can be used over most or all of the geographical area of the Earth.  In order for the phone to communicate with a satellite using a small [[omnidirectional antenna]], first-generation systems use satellites in [[low Earth orbit]], about {{convert|400-700|mi|km|sigfig=2}} above the surface.  With an orbital period of about 100 minutes, a satellite can only be in view of a phone for about 4 – 15 minutes, so the call is "handed off" to another satellite when one passes beyond the local horizon. Therefore, large numbers of satellites, about 40 to 70, are required to ensure that at least one satellite is in view continuously from each point on Earth.  Other satphone systems use satellites in [[geostationary orbit]] in which only a few satellites are needed, but these cannot be used at high latitudes because of terrestrial interference.<ref name="Chandler">{{Cite web |last=Chandler |first=Nathan |date=13 February 2013 |title=How Satellite Phones Work |url=https://electronics.howstuffworks.com/gadgets/travel/satellite-phone.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220902191813/https://electronics.howstuffworks.com/gadgets/travel/satellite-phone.htm |archive-date=2 September 2022 |access-date=2 September 2022 |website=howstuffworks.com |publisher=HowStuffWorks}}</ref><ref name="TW">{{Cite web |title=Satellite Phone : Functioning/Working Of Satellite Phone |url=https://www.tutorialsweb.com/satellite-phones/satellite-phones-2.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155810/https://www.tutorialsweb.com/satellite-phones/satellite-phones-2.htm |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=2 September 2022 |website=tutorialsweb.com |publisher=Tutorials Web}}</ref>
* [[Cordless phone]] – a [[landline telephone]] in which the [[handset]] is portable and communicates with the rest of the phone by a short-range [[Duplex (telecommunications)|full duplex]] radio link, instead of being attached by a cord.  Both the handset and the base station have low-power radio transceivers that handle the short-range bidirectional radio link.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=McComb |first=Gordon |date=October 1982 |title=Never Miss a Call: PS Buyer's Guide to Cordless Phones |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ia91vNwYgLIC |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155706/https://books.google.com/books?id=ia91vNwYgLIC |archive-date=2024-10-03 |access-date=2022-09-07 |magazine=Popular Science |pages=84–85 |via=Google Books}}</ref> {{As of|2022}}, cordless phones in most nations use the [[DECT]] transmission standard.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Guy |first=Nick |date=13 July 2022 |title=Wirecutter: The Best Cordless Phone |url=https://www.nytimes.com/wirecutter/reviews/best-cordless-phone/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220907195609/https://www.nytimes.com/wirecutter/reviews/best-cordless-phone/ |archive-date=7 September 2022 |access-date=7 September 2022 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

[[File:Ascon_SE_660_radio.jpg|thumb|Two-way radio in a [[fire truck]] used by firefighters to communicate with their dispatcher]]

* [[Land mobile radio system]] – short-range mobile or portable [[half-duplex]] radio transceivers operating in the VHF or UHF band that can be used without a license.  They are often installed in vehicles, with the mobile units communicating with a dispatcher at a fixed [[base station]]. Special systems with reserved frequencies are used by [[first responder]] services; police, fire, ambulance, and emergency services, and other government services.  Other systems are made for use by commercial firms such as taxi and delivery services.  VHF systems use channels in the range 30–50&nbsp;MHz and 150–172&nbsp;MHz.  UHF systems use the 450–470&nbsp;MHz band and in some areas the 470–512&nbsp;MHz range.  In general, VHF systems have a longer range than UHF but require longer antennas. AM or FM modulation is mainly used, but digital systems such as [[Digital mobile radio|DMR]] are being introduced.  The radiated power is typically limited to 4 watts.<ref name="HowCellPhonesWork" /> These systems have a fairly limited range, usually {{convert|3 to 20|miles|km|sigfig=2}} depending on terrain. [[Repeater|Repeaters]] installed on tall buildings, hills, or mountain peaks are often used to increase the range when it is desired to cover a larger area than line-of-sight.  Examples of land mobile systems are [[Citizens Band|CB]], [[Family Radio Service|FRS]], [[GMRS]], and [[MURS]].  Modern digital systems, called [[trunked radio systems]], have a digital channel management system using a control channel that automatically assigns frequency channels to user groups.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://www.usfa.fema.gov/downloads/pdf/publications/voice_radio_communications_guide_for_the_fire_service.pdf |title=Voice Radio Communications Guide for the Fire Service |last=U.S. Fire Administration |date=June 2016 |publisher=Federal Emergency Management Agency |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=33–34 |access-date=7 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220907201749/https://www.usfa.fema.gov/downloads/pdf/publications/voice_radio_communications_guide_for_the_fire_service.pdf |archive-date=7 September 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[Walkie-talkie]] – a battery-powered portable handheld half-duplex two-way radio, used in land mobile radio systems.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sterling |first=Christopher H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RBC2nY1rp5MC&pg=PA504 |title=Military Communications: From Ancient Times to the 21st Century |publisher=ABC-CLIO |year=2008 |isbn=978-1851097326 |pages=503–504}}</ref>

* [[Airband]] – Half-duplex radio system used by aircraft pilots to talk to other aircraft and ground-based [[air traffic controllers]]. This vital system is the main communication channel for [[air traffic control]]. For most communication in overland flights in [[Air corridor|air corridors]] a VHF-AM system using channels between 108 and 137&nbsp;MHz in the [[VHF]] band is used.  This system has a typical transmission range of {{convert|200|miles|km|sigfig=2}} for aircraft flying at cruising altitude.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://us-afc.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/AFC-Manual-Rev-B-May-20-2012.pdf |title=Aeronautical Frequency Committee Manual |publisher=Aviation Spectrum Resources Inc. |issue=61604 Rev. B |publication-date=2012}}</ref><ref name="Smeter network 2011">{{Cite web |title=Aviation Radio Bands and Frequencies |url=http://www.smeter.net/spectrum/aviation.php |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040212142911/http://www.smeter.net/spectrum/aviation.php |archive-date=12 February 2004 |access-date=16 February 2011 |publisher=Smeter network 2011}}</ref> For flights in more remote areas, such as transoceanic airline flights, aircraft use the [[High frequency|HF]] band or channels on the [[Inmarsat]] or [[Iridium]] satphone satellites.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://www.icao.int/WACAF/Documents/Meetings/2019/SAT24/SAT%2024%20WP%2017e%20_APP%20E_NAT%20Doc%20007%20%20(EN)%20-%20Edition%20V.2019-2_eff.pdf |title=North Atlantic Operations and Airspace Manual |date=28 March 2019 |publisher=ICAO European and North Atlantic Office |issue=V.2019–2 |access-date=4 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220808121543/https://www.icao.int/WACAF/Documents/Meetings/2019/SAT24/SAT%2024%20WP%2017e%20_APP%20E_NAT%20Doc%20007%20%20(EN)%20-%20Edition%20V.2019-2_eff.pdf |archive-date=8 August 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>  Military aircraft also use a dedicated UHF-AM band from 225.0 to 399.95&nbsp;MHz.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Van Horn |first=Larry |title=The Military VHF/UHF Spectrum |url=http://www.monitoringtimes.com/html/mtMilVHF.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003155707/http://www.monitoringtimes.com/html/mtMilVHF.html |archive-date=2024-10-03 |access-date=2022-09-04 |magazine=Monitoring Times}}</ref>

[[File:Maritime_VHF_Sailor_type.jpg|thumb|VHF marine radio on a ship]]

* [[Marine radio]] – medium-range transceivers on ships, used for ship-to-ship, ship-to-air, and ship-to-shore communication with [[Harbormaster|harbormasters]] They use FM channels between 156 and 174&nbsp;MHz in the [[VHF]] band with up to 25 watts power, giving them a range of about {{convert|60|miles|km|sigfig=2}}. Some channels are [[half-duplex]] and some are [[full-duplex]], to be compatible with the telephone network, to allow users to make telephone calls through a marine operator.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fletcher |first=Sue |title=A Boater's Guide to VHF and GMDSS |publisher=International Marine/McGraw-Hill |year=2002 |isbn=0071388028 |location=Camden, Maine |oclc=48674566}}</ref>
* [[Amateur radio]] – long-range half-duplex two-way radio used by hobbyists for non-commercial purposes: recreational radio contacts with other amateurs, volunteer emergency communication during disasters, contests, and experimentation. [[Radio amateurs]] must hold an [[amateur radio license]] and are given a unique [[callsign]] that must be used as an identifier in transmissions.  Amateur radio is restricted to small frequency bands, the [[amateur radio bands]], spaced throughout the radio spectrum starting at 136&nbsp;kHz.  Within these bands, amateurs are allowed the freedom to transmit on any frequency using a wide variety of voice modulation methods, along with other forms of communication, such as [[slow-scan television]] (SSTV), and [[radioteletype]] (RTTY).  Additionally, amateurs are among the only radio operators still using [[Morse code]] [[radiotelegraphy]].<ref>{{Cite book |title=The ARRL Handbook for Radio Communications 2017 |date=2016 |publisher=American Radio Relay League |isbn=978-1625950628 |edition=94th |location=Newington, Connecticut |oclc=961215964}}</ref>
* ''[[Scanner (radio)|Scanner]]'' - a receiver that continuously monitors multiple frequencies or [[Radio channel|radio channels]] by stepping through the channels repeatedly, listening briefly to each channel for a transmission. When a transmitter is found the receiver stops at that channel. Scanners are used to monitor emergency police, fire, and ambulance frequencies, as well as other two way radio frequencies such as [[citizens band]]. Scanning capabilities have also become a standard feature in communications receivers, walkie-talkies, and other two-way radios.
* ''[[Communications receiver]]'' or ''[[shortwave receiver]]'' - a general purpose audio receiver covering the [[Low frequency|LF]], [[Medium frequency|MF]], [[shortwave]] ([[High frequency|HF]]), and [[VHF]] bands. Used mostly with a separate shortwave transmitter for two-way voice communication in communication stations, [[amateur radio]] stations, and for [[shortwave listening]].

=== One-way voice communication ===
One way, unidirectional radio transmission is called ''[[Simplex communication|simplex]]''.

* [[Baby monitor]] – a crib-side appliance for parents of infants that transmits the baby's sounds to a receiver carried by the parent, so they can monitor the baby while they are in other parts of the house.<ref name="HSW1">{{Cite web |last=Brain |first=Marshall |date=11 February 2021 |title=Radio basics: Real life examples |url=https://electronics.howstuffworks.com/radio.htm#pt4 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160102215734/http://www.howstuffworks.com/radio.htm#pt4 |archive-date=2 January 2016 |access-date=27 August 2022 |website=How radio works |publisher=How Stuff Works website}}</ref> The wavebands used vary by region, but analog baby monitors generally transmit with low power in the 16, 9.3–49.9 or 900&nbsp;MHz wavebands, and digital systems in the 2.4&nbsp;GHz waveband.<ref>{{Cite report |url=http://www.bccdc.ca/resource-gallery/Documents/Educational%20Materials/EH/Radiofrequency-Toolkit.pdf |title=Radiofrequency Toolkit for Environmental Health Practitioners |publisher=British Columbia Centre for Disease Control/National Collaborating Centre for Environmental Health |location=Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada |page=26 |isbn=978-1926933481 |access-date=2022-09-09 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221009/http://www.bccdc.ca/resource-gallery/Documents/Educational%20Materials/EH/Radiofrequency-Toolkit.pdf |archive-date=2022-10-09 |url-status=live}}</ref> Many baby monitors have duplex channels so the parent can talk to the baby, and cameras to show video of the baby.<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=24 April 2016 |title=Best Baby Monitor Buying Guide |url=https://www.consumerreports.org/babies-kids/baby-monitors/buying-guide/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220909192535/https://www.consumerreports.org/babies-kids/baby-monitors/buying-guide/ |archive-date=9 September 2022 |access-date=9 September 2022 |magazine=Consumer Reports |language=en-US}}</ref>
* [[Wireless microphone]] – a battery-powered microphone with a short-range transmitter that is handheld or worn on a person's body which transmits its sound by radio to a nearby receiver unit connected to a sound system.  Wireless microphones are used by public speakers, performers, and television personalities so they can move freely without trailing a microphone cord. Traditionally, analog models transmit in FM on unused portions of the television broadcast frequencies in the VHF and UHF bands.  Some models transmit on two frequency channels for [[diversity reception]] to prevent [[Null (radio)|nulls]] from interrupting transmission as the performer moves around.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Eargle |first=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JnkqBgAAQBAJ |title=The Microphone Book |date=2005 |publisher=Focal Press |isbn=978-1136118067 |edition=2nd |location=Oxford |pages=142–151 |chapter=Overview of Wireless Microphone Technology |access-date=2022-09-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160240/https://books.google.com/books?id=JnkqBgAAQBAJ |archive-date=2024-10-03 |url-status=live |via=Google Books}}</ref> While some consumer models use digital modulation in the 900 MHz, 2.4 GHz, or 6 GHz [[ISM bands]], most professional wireless microphone and in-ear monitor (IEM) systems operate in the [[UHF]] TV band (typically 470–702 MHz).<ref name="OfcomUHF">{{cite web |last1=Ofcom |title=Wireless microphones and monitors |url=https://www.ofcom.org.uk/spectrum/radio-equipment/mics-monitors |access-date=2025-12-28 |website=Ofcom.org.uk |date=11 May 2015 |language=en}}</ref> Modern developments include Wireless Multichannel Audio Systems (WMAS), which utilize wideband transmission to support high channel density within a single radio frequency carrier. While European [[ETSI]] standards have supported WMAS for several years<ref name="ETSI_WMAS">{{cite web |last1=ETSI |title=ETSI EN 300 422-1 V2.2.1: Wireless Microphones; Audio PMSE up to 3 GHz; Part 1: Audio PMSE Equipment up to 3 GHz |url=https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_en/300400_300499/30042201/02.02.01_60/en_30042201v020201p.pdf |access-date=2025-12-28 |publisher=European Telecommunications Standards Institute |date=2021-11-12}}</ref>, the U.S. [[Federal Communications Commission]] (FCC) officially adopted rules in February 2024 to allow WMAS operation in the United States.<ref name="FCC2024WMAS">{{cite press release |last1=FCC |title=FCC Expands Opportunities for Wireless Microphone Users |url=https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-400524A1.pdf |access-date=2025-12-28 |publisher=Federal Communications Commission |date=2024-02-15}}</ref> This regulatory change led to the introduction of wideband digital platforms such as [[Sennheiser]]’s Spectera<ref name="SennheiserSpectera">{{cite web |last1=Sennheiser |title=Sennheiser launches Spectera: The world's first wideband, bidirectional wireless ecosystem |url=https://en-de.sennheiser.com/newsroom/sennheiser-launches-spectera |access-date=2025-12-28 |website=Sennheiser Newsroom |date=2024-09-13}}</ref> and [[Shure]]’s Axient Digital PSM (ADPSM)<ref name="ShureADPSM">{{cite web |last1=Shure |title=Shure Introduces Axient Digital PSM Wireless In-Ear Monitoring System |url=https://www.shure.com/en-US/newsroom/axient-digital-psm |access-date=2025-12-28 |website=Shure.com |date=2024-10-22}}</ref>, which allow for bidirectional audio and increased spectral efficiency at large-scale events.

== Data communication ==
{{further|Data transmission|Telemetry|Wireless communication}}

* [[Wireless networking]] – automated radio links which transmit digital data between computers and other wireless devices using radio waves, linking the devices together transparently in a [[computer network]].  Computer networks can transmit any form of data: in addition to email and web pages, they also carry [[phone calls]] ([[VoIP]]), audio, and video content (called [[streaming media]]).  Security is more of an issue for wireless networks than for wired networks since anyone nearby with a wireless modem can access the signal and attempt to log in.
