The radio signals of wireless networks are [[encrypted]] using [[Wi-Fi Protected Access|WPA]].<ref name="Lewis-Davis">{{Cite book |last1=Lewis |first1=Barry D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a3_S-c8nfqsC&q=Wireless+networking+WPA |title=Wireless Networks For Dummies |last2=Davis |first2=Peter T. |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=2004 |isbn=978-0764579776 |access-date=12 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160214/https://books.google.com/books?id=a3_S-c8nfqsC&q=Wireless+networking+WPA#v=snippet&q=Wireless%20networking%20WPA&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
** [[File:Wireless_network.jpg|thumb|A laptop (with [[Wi-Fi]] module) and a typical home [[wireless router]] ''(on the right)'' connecting it to the Internet. The laptop [[Droste effect|shows its own photo]]]][[Wireless LAN]] (''wireless local area network'' or ''[[Wi-Fi]]'') – based on the [[IEEE 802.11]] standards, these are the most widely used computer networks, used to implement [[local area networks]] without cables, linking computers, laptops, cell phones, [[video game consoles]], [[smart TVs]] and [[Computer printer|printers]] in a home or office together, and to a [[wireless router]] connecting them to the Internet with a wire or cable connection.  Wireless routers in public places like libraries, hotels and coffee shops create [[wireless access points]] ([[Hotspot (Wi-Fi)|hotspots]]) to allow the public to access the Internet with portable devices like [[smartphones]], [[Tablet computer|tablets]] or [[laptops]].  Each device exchanges data using a [[Wireless network interface controller|wireless modem]] (wireless network interface controller), an automated [[microwave]] transmitter and receiver with an omnidirectional antenna that works in the background, exchanging [[data packets]] with the router.  Wi-Fi uses channels in the 2.4&nbsp;GHz and 5&nbsp;GHz [[ISM bands]] with OFDM ([[orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing]]) modulation to transmit data at high rates.  The transmitters in Wi-Fi modems are limited to a radiated power of 200&nbsp;mW to 1&nbsp;watt, depending on country. They have a maximum indoor range of about {{convert|150|ft|m|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} on 2.4&nbsp;GHz and {{convert|50|ft|m|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} on 5&nbsp;GHz.<ref name="Lowe">{{Cite book |last=Lowe |first=Doug |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LiHxDwAAQBAJ&q=Wireless+WAN+basics |title=Networking For Dummies |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=2020 |isbn=978-1119748670 |access-date=12 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160215/https://books.google.com/books?id=LiHxDwAAQBAJ&q=Wireless+WAN+basics#v=snippet&q=Wireless%20WAN%20basics&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
** [[File:USI_router.jpg|thumb|Neighborhood wireless WAN router on telephone pole]][[Wireless WAN]] (wireless wide area network, WWAN) – a variety of technologies that provide wireless internet access over a wider area than Wi-Fi networks do – from an office building to a campus to a neighborhood, or to an entire city.  The most common technologies used are: [[Cellular modem|cellular modems]], that exchange computer data by radio with [[cell towers]]; satellite internet access; and lower frequencies in the UHF band, which have a longer range than Wi-Fi frequencies.  Since WWAN networks are much more expensive and complicated to administer than Wi-Fi networks, their use so far has generally been limited to private networks operated by large corporations.<ref name="Lowe" />
** [[Bluetooth]] – a very short-range wireless interface on a portable wireless device used as a substitute for a wire or cable connection, mainly to exchange files between portable devices and connect cellphones and music players with wireless [[headphones]].  In the most widely used mode, transmission power is limited to 1&nbsp;milliwatt, giving it a very short range of up to 10 m (30 feet).  The system uses [[frequency-hopping spread spectrum]] transmission, in which successive [[data packets]] are transmitted in a pseudorandom order on one of 79 1&nbsp;MHz Bluetooth channels between 2.4 and 2.83&nbsp;GHz in the [[ISM band]]. This allows Bluetooth networks to operate in the presence of [[Radio noise|noise]], other wireless devices and other Bluetooth networks using the same frequencies, since the chance of another device attempting to transmit on the same frequency at the same time as the Bluetooth modem is low.  In the case of such a "collision", the Bluetooth modem just retransmits the data packet on another frequency.<ref name="Muller">{{Cite book |last=Muller |first=Nathan J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0qv4KbasX7wC&q=bluetooth&pg=PA45 |title=Networking A to Z |date=2002 |publisher=McGraw-Hill Professional |isbn=978-0071429139 |pages=45–47 |access-date=12 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624205933/https://books.google.com/books?id=0qv4KbasX7wC&q=bluetooth&pg=PA45 |archive-date=24 June 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>
** [[Packet radio]] – a long-distance [[peer-to-peer]] [[wireless ad-hoc network]] in which [[data packets]] are exchanged between computer-controlled [[Radio modem|radio modems]] (transmitter/receivers) called nodes, which may be separated by miles, and maybe mobile.  Each node only communicates with neighboring nodes, so packets of data are passed from node to node until they reach their destination using the [[X.25]] network protocol. Packet radio systems are used to a limited degree by commercial telecommunications companies and by the [[amateur radio]] community.<ref name="Silver">{{Cite book |last=Silver |first=H. Ward |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EcbjKvhgPLsC&dq=Packet+radio&pg=SA2-PA11 |title=The ARRL Extra Class License Manual for Ham Radio |publisher=American Radio Relay League |year=2008 |isbn=978-0872591356 |access-date=12 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160216/https://books.google.com/books?id=EcbjKvhgPLsC&dq=Packet+radio&pg=SA2-PA11#v=onepage&q=Packet%20radio&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* Text messaging (texting) – this is a service on cell phones, allowing a user to type a short alphanumeric message and send it to another phone number, and the text is displayed on the recipient's phone screen.  It is based on the [[Short Message Service]] (SMS) which transmits using spare bandwidth on the control radio channel used by cell phones to handle background functions like dialing and cell handoffs. Due to technical limitations of the channel, text messages are limited to 160 alphanumeric characters.<ref name="Hillebrand">{{Cite book |last=Hillebrand |first=Friedhelm |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YPgfNaoYHUsC&q=Text+messaging++160+char |title=Short Message Service (SMS): The Creation of Personal Global Text Messaging |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=2010 |isbn=978-0470689936 |access-date=12 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160218/https://books.google.com/books?id=YPgfNaoYHUsC&q=Text+messaging++160+char#v=snippet&q=Text%20messaging%20%20160%20char&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Parabolic_antennas.JPG|thumb|[[Parabolic antenna|Parabolic antennas]] of microwave relay links on tower in Australia]]

* [[Microwave relay]] – a long-distance high bandwidth point-to-point digital data transmission link consisting of a microwave transmitter connected to a [[dish antenna]] that transmits a beam of [[microwaves]] to another dish antenna and receiver. Since the antennas must be in line-of-sight, distances are limited by the visual horizon to {{convert|30-40|miles|km|sigfig=2}}. Microwave links are used for private business data, wide area computer networks (WANs), and by telephone companies to transmit long-distance phone calls and television signals between cities.<ref name="McGregor-Driscoll-Mcdowell">{{Cite book |last1=McGregor |first1=Michael A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m6dYCwAAQBAJ&dq=Microwave+relay+%E2%80%93&pg=PT224 |title=Head's Broadcasting in America: A Survey of Electronic Media |last2=Driscoll |first2=Paul D. |last3=Mcdowell |first3=Walter |publisher=Routledge |year=2016 |isbn=978-1317347927 |access-date=12 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160218/https://books.google.com/books?id=m6dYCwAAQBAJ&dq=Microwave+relay+%E2%80%93&pg=PT224#v=onepage&q=Microwave%20relay%20%E2%80%93&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="EIA">{{Cite web |last=Radio-Electronics-Television Manufacturers Association. Engineering Department |year=1955 |title=Microwave Relay Systems for Communications |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-OP2xwEACAAJ&q=Microwave+relay+%E2%80%93 |access-date=12 September 2022 |publisher=Electronic Industries Association}}</ref>
* [[Telemetry]] – automated one-way (simplex) transmission of measurements and operation data from a remote process or device to a receiver for monitoring.  Telemetry is used for in-flight monitoring of missiles, drones, satellites, and [[weather balloon]] [[radiosondes]], sending scientific data back to Earth from interplanetary spacecraft, communicating with electronic biomedical sensors implanted in the human body, and [[well logging]]. Multiple channels of data are often transmitted using [[frequency-division multiplexing]] or [[time-division multiplexing]].<ref name="Bailey">{{Cite book |last=Bailey |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=K-wxbN3rjMwC&dq=radio+telemetry+fundamentals&pg=PR4 |title=Practical Radio Engineering and Telemetry for Industry |publisher=Elsevier |year=2003 |isbn=978-0080473895 |access-date=12 September 2022}}</ref> Telemetry is starting to be used in consumer applications such as:
** [[Automated meter reading]] – [[Electricity meter|electric power meters]], [[water meters]], and [[Gas meter|gas meters]] that, when triggered by an interrogation signal, transmit their readings by radio to a utility reader vehicle at the curb, to eliminate the need for an employee to go on the customer's property to manually read the meter.{{cn|date=June 2025}}
** [[Electronic toll collection]] – on [[toll roads]], an alternative to manual collection of tolls at a toll booth, in which a [[transponder]] in a vehicle, when triggered by a roadside transmitter, transmits a signal to a roadside receiver to register the vehicle's use of the road, enabling the owner to be billed for the toll.<ref name="Bonsor-2001a">{{Cite web |last=Bonsor |first=Kevin |date=28 August 2001 |title=How E-ZPass Works |url=https://auto.howstuffworks.com/e-zpass.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220912151122/https://auto.howstuffworks.com/e-zpass.htm |archive-date=12 September 2022 |access-date=12 September 2022 |website=howstuffworks.com |publisher=HowStuff Works}}</ref>

[[File:RFID_Chip_001.JPG|thumb|RFID tag from a DVD]]

* [[Radio Frequency Identification]] (RFID) – identification tags containing a tiny radio transponder ([[Radio receiver|receiver]] and [[transmitter]]) which are attached to merchandise.  When it receives an interrogation pulse of radio waves from a nearby reader unit, the tag transmits back an ID number, which can be used to inventory goods.  Passive tags, the most common type, have a chip powered by the radio energy received from the reader, rectified by a diode, and can be as small as a grain of rice.  They are incorporated in products, clothes, railroad cars, library books, airline baggage tags and are implanted under the skin in pets and livestock ([[Microchip implant (animal)|microchip implant]]) and even people. Privacy concerns have been addressed with tags that use [[encrypted]] signals and [[authenticate]] the reader before responding.  Passive tags use 125–134&nbsp;kHz, 13, 900&nbsp;MHz and 2.4 and 5&nbsp;GHz [[ISM bands]] and have a short range.  Active tags, powered by a battery, are larger but can transmit a stronger signal, giving them a range of hundreds of meters.<ref name="Hunt-Puglia-Puglia">{{Cite book |last1=Hunt |first1=V. Daniel |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZCHiHqL6QKkC&q=Radio+Frequency+Identification |title=RFID: A Guide to Radio Frequency Identification |last2=Puglia |first2=Albert |last3=Puglia |first3=Mike |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=2007 |isbn=978-0470112243 |access-date=12 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160734/https://books.google.com/books?id=ZCHiHqL6QKkC&q=Radio+Frequency+Identification#v=snippet&q=Radio%20Frequency%20Identification&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[Communication with submarines|Submarine communication]] – When submerged, [[submarines]] are cut off from all ordinary radio communication with their military command authorities by the conductive seawater.  However radio waves of low enough frequencies, in the [[VLF]] (30 to 3&nbsp;kHz) and [[Extremely low frequency|ELF]] (below 3&nbsp;kHz) bands are able to penetrate seawater.  Navies operate large shore transmitting stations with power output in the megawatt range to transmit [[encrypted]] messages to their submarines in the world's oceans.  Due to the small bandwidth, these systems cannot transmit voice, only text messages at a slow data rate. The communication channel is one-way, since the long antennas needed to transmit VLF or ELF waves cannot fit on a submarine.  [[VLF]] transmitters use miles long wire antennas like [[Umbrella antenna|umbrella antennas]].  A few nations use ELF transmitters operating around 80&nbsp;Hz, which can communicate with submarines at lower depths.  These use even larger antennas called [[Ground dipole|ground dipoles]], consisting of two [[Ground (electricity)|ground]] (Earth) connections {{convert|23-60|km|miles|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} apart, linked by overhead transmission lines to a power plant transmitter.<ref name="White">{{Cite web |last=White |first=Ryan |date=17 December 2021 |title=How do submarines communicate with the outside world? |url=https://navalpost.com/how-do-submarines-communicate-with-the-outside-world/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160739/https://navalpost.com/how-do-submarines-communicate-with-the-outside-world/ |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=12 September 2022 |website=navalpost.com |publisher=Naval Post}}</ref><ref name="NRR">{{Cite web |year=1974 |title=Naval Research Reviews, Vol. 27 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QANVAAAAMAAJ&dq=Submarine+communication+grounded+dipole&pg=PA5 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160801/https://books.google.com/books?id=QANVAAAAMAAJ&dq=Submarine+communication+grounded+dipole&pg=PA5#v=onepage&q=Submarine%20communication%20grounded%20dipole&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=12 September 2022 |publisher=Superintendent of Government Documents}}</ref>

== Space communication ==
[[File:ЦКС_Дубна_ГПКС_-6.jpg|thumb|[[Earth station|Satellite Communications Center]] [[Dubna]] in Russia<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ground infrastructure |url=https://eng.rscc.ru/space/centry-kosmicheskoj-svyazi/cks-dubna/ |website=[[Russian Satellite Communications Company]]}}</ref>]]
This is radio communication between a [[spacecraft]] and an Earth-based ground station, or another spacecraft.  Communication with spacecraft involves the longest transmission distances of any radio links, up to billions of kilometers for [[interplanetary spacecraft]].  In order to receive the weak signals from distant spacecraft, [[Satellite ground station|satellite ground stations]] use large [[Parabolic antenna|parabolic "dish" antennas]] up to {{convert|25|m|ft|sigfig=2}} in diameter and extremely sensitive receivers. High frequencies in the [[microwave]] band are used, since microwaves pass through the [[ionosphere]] without [[refraction]], and at microwave frequencies the [[High-gain antenna|high-gain antennas]] needed to focus the radio energy into a narrow beam pointed at the receiver are small and take up a minimum of space in a satellite. Portions of the [[UHF]], [[L band|L]], [[C band (IEEE)|C]], [[S band|S]], [[Ku band|k<sub>u</sub>]] and [[Ka band|k<sub>a</sub> band]] are allocated for space communication.  A radio link that transmits data from the Earth's surface to a spacecraft is called an [[uplink]], while a link that transmits data from the spacecraft to the ground is called a downlink.<ref name="NASA3">{{Cite web |date=16 October 2021 |title=State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology, 9.0 - Communications |url=https://www.nasa.gov/smallsat-institute/sst-soa/communications |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160739/https://www.nasa.gov/smallsat-institute/sst-soa/soa-communications/ |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=11 September 2022 |website=nasa.gov |publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration}}</ref>
[[File:Azərbaycan_peyki_-_VOA.jpg|thumb|Communications satellite belonging to [[Azerbaijan]]]]

* [[Communication satellite]] – an [[artificial satellite]] used as a telecommunications relay to transmit data between widely separated points on Earth.  These are used because the [[microwaves]] used for telecommunications travel by [[Line-of-sight propagation|line of sight]] and so cannot propagate around the curve of the Earth. {{as of|2021|1|1}}, there were 2,224 communications satellites in Earth orbit.<ref name="UCSdatabase">{{Cite web |date=1 January 2021 |title=UCS Satellite Database |url=https://www.ucsusa.org/resources/satellite-database#.W7WcwpMza9Y |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191220002901/https://ucsusa.org/resources/satellite-database#.W7WcwpMza9Y |archive-date=20 December 2019 |access-date=21 May 2021 |publisher=Union of Concerned Scientists}}</ref>  Most are in [[geostationary]] orbit {{convert|22200|mi|km|sigfig=3}} above the [[equator]], so that the satellite appears stationary at the same point in the sky, so the satellite dish antennas of ground stations can be aimed permanently at that spot and do not have to move to track it.  In a [[satellite ground station]] a microwave transmitter and large satellite dish antenna transmit a microwave uplink beam to the satellite.  The uplink signal carries many channels of telecommunications traffic, such as long-distance telephone calls, television programs, and internet signals, using a technique called [[frequency-division multiplexing]] (FDM).  On the satellite, a [[Transponder (satellite communications)|transponder]] receives the signal, translates it to a different downlink frequency to avoid interfering with the uplink signal, and retransmits it down to another ground station, which may be widely separated from the first.  There the downlink signal is demodulated and the telecommunications traffic it carries is sent to its local destinations through landlines.  Communication satellites typically have several dozen transponders on different frequencies, which are leased by different users.<ref name="Marsten">{{Cite book |last=Marsten |first=Richard B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NEWoBQAAQBAJ&q=Communication+satellite |title=Communication Satellite Systems Technology |publisher=Academic Press |year=2014 |isbn=978-1483276816 |access-date=11 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160737/https://books.google.com/books?id=NEWoBQAAQBAJ&q=Communication+satellite#v=snippet&q=Communication%20satellite&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[Direct broadcast satellite]] – a geostationary communication satellite that transmits retail programming directly to receivers in subscriber's homes and vehicles on Earth, in [[satellite radio]] and TV systems.  It uses a higher transmitter power than other communication satellites, to allow the signal to be received by consumers with a small unobtrusive antenna.  For example, satellite television uses downlink frequencies from 12.2 to 12.7&nbsp;GHz in the [[Ku band|k<sub>u</sub> band]] transmitted at 100 to 250 watts, which can be received by relatively small {{convert|43-80|cm|inch|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} [[satellite dishes]] mounted on the outside of buildings.<ref name="rfwirelessworld">{{Cite web |title=Satellite TV-Direct Broadcast Satellite System, DBS TV |url=https://www.rfwireless-world.com/Tutorials/satellite-TV-basics.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160739/https://www.rfwireless-world.com/Tutorials/satellite-TV-basics.html |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=11 September 2022 |website=rfwireless-world.com |publisher=RF Wireless World}}</ref>

== Medicine ==
{{main|Medical applications of radio frequency}}
Medical applications of radio frequency (RF) energy, in the form of [[electromagnetic waves]] ([[radio waves]]) or electrical currents, have existed for over 125 years,<ref>{{cite book |author1=Ruey J. Sung |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=S1fWhl2c5zIC&q=rf+coagulation+75-years&pg=PA153 |title=Fundamental approaches to the management of cardiac arrhythmias |author2=Michael R. Lauer |publisher=Springer |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-7923-6559-4 |page=153 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905205035/https://books.google.com/books?id=S1fWhl2c5zIC&pg=PA153&dq=rf+coagulation+75-years&lr=&as_brr=3&ei=IIhuSpfBJ6aqlQT-n7nmDg |archive-date=2015-09-05 |url-status=live |name-list-style=amp}}</ref> and now include [[diathermy]], [[hyperthermy]] treatment of cancer, [[electrosurgery]] scalpels used to cut and cauterize in operations, and [[radiofrequency ablation]].<ref>{{cite book |author1=Melvin A. Shiffman |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w1fQK21WK28C&q=rf+coagulation+sleep-apnea&pg=RA1-PA157 |title=Simplified Facial Rejuvenation |author2=Sid J. Mirrafati |author3=Samuel M. Lam |author4=Chelso G. Cueteaux |publisher=Springer |year=2007 |isbn=978-3-540-71096-7 |page=157}}</ref> [[Magnetic resonance imaging]] (MRI) uses radio frequency fields to generate images of the human body.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bethge |first=K. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EAVYCfcQCxEC&q=%C2%A0+Magnetic+resonance+imaging+%28MRI%29+uses+radio+frequency+waves+to+generate+images+of+the+human+body.&pg=PA101 |title=Medical Applications of Nuclear Physics |date=2004-04-27 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=9783540208051 |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180501015943/https://books.google.com/books?id=EAVYCfcQCxEC&pg=PA101&dq=%C2%A0+Magnetic+resonance+imaging+(MRI)+uses+radio+frequency+waves+to+generate+images+of+the+human+body.&hl=en&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwjlrrL-mKfVAhVMy1QKHUc9D5UQ6AEIJjAA#v=onepage&q=%C2%A0%20Magnetic%20resonance%20imaging%20(MRI)%20uses%20radio%20frequency%20waves%20to%20generate%20images%20of%20the%20human%20body.&f=false |archive-date=2018-05-01 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Other applications ==

=== Radar ===
{{main|Radar}}
[[File:US_Navy_120208-N-TU894-022_Air-Traffic_Controller_2nd_Class_Gregory_Clemmons_stands_the_departure_position_watch_as_Air-Traffic_Controller_3rd_Clas.jpg|thumb|Military [[air traffic controller]] on US Navy aircraft carrier monitors aircraft on radar screen]]
[[Radar]] is a [[radiolocation]] method used to locate and track aircraft, spacecraft, missiles, ships, vehicles, and also to map weather patterns and terrain. A radar set consists of a transmitter and receiver.<ref name="HowRadarWorks">{{Cite web |last=Brain |first=Marshall |date=2020 |title=How radar works |url=https://science.howstuffworks.com/radar.htm?srch_tag=swsu5cd23kj6x6xnw4jfrts6awdrk5sg |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003160741/https://science.howstuffworks.com/radar.htm?srch_tag=swsu5cd23kj6x6xnw4jfrts6awdrk5sg |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=3 September 2022 |publisher=How Stuff Works}}</ref><ref name="Skolnik">{{Cite encyclopedia |title=Radar |encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica online |publisher=Encyclopædia Britannica Inc. |url=https://www.britannica.com/technology/radar |last=Skolnik |first=Merrill |date=2021 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161248/https://www.britannica.com/technology/radar |archive-date=3 October 2024 |accessdate=3 September 2022}}</ref>  The transmitter emits a narrow beam of radio waves which is swept around the surrounding space.  When the beam strikes a target object, radio waves are reflected back to the receiver.  The direction of the beam reveals the object's location.  Since radio waves travel at a constant speed close to the [[speed of light]], by measuring the brief time delay between the outgoing pulse and the received "echo", the range to the target can be calculated.  The targets are often displayed graphically on a map display called a ''radar screen''.  [[Doppler radar]] can measure a moving object's velocity, by measuring the change in frequency of the return radio waves due to the [[Doppler effect]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=JetStream |url=https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161249/https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream |archive-date=2024-10-03 |access-date=2023-06-14 |website=www.noaa.gov}}</ref>

Radar sets mainly use high frequencies in the [[microwave]] bands, because these frequencies create strong reflections from objects the size of vehicles and can be focused into narrow beams with compact antennas.<ref name="Skolnik" />  [[Parabolic antenna|Parabolic (dish) antennas]] are widely used.  In most radars the transmitting antenna also serves as the receiving antenna; this is called a ''[[monostatic radar]]''.  A radar which uses separate transmitting and receiving antennas is called a ''[[bistatic radar]]''.<ref name="Chernyak">{{Cite book |last=Chernyak |first=Victor S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0bEU2oBzMJEC&q=Bistatic+&pg=PA149 |title=Fundamentals of multisite radar systems: multistatic radars and multiradar systems |publisher=CRC Press |year=1998 |isbn=9056991655 |pages=3, 149 |access-date=2022-09-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161400/https://books.google.com/books?id=0bEU2oBzMJEC&q=Bistatic+&pg=PA149#v=snippet&q=Bistatic&f=false |archive-date=2024-10-03 |url-status=live}}</ref>
[[File:ASR-9_Radar_Antenna.jpg|thumb|ASR-8 airport surveillance radar antenna.  It rotates once every 4.8 seconds.  The rectangular antenna on top is the secondary radar.]]

* [[Airport surveillance radar]] – In aviation, radar is the main tool of [[air traffic control]].  A rotating dish antenna sweeps a vertical fan-shaped beam of microwaves around the airspace and the radar set shows the location of aircraft as "blips" of light on a display called a radar screen. Airport radar operates at 2.7 – 2.9&nbsp;GHz in the microwave [[S band]].  In large airports the radar image is displayed on multiple screens in an operations room called the TRACON ([[Terminal Radar Approach Control]]), where [[air traffic controllers]] direct the aircraft by radio to maintain safe aircraft separation.<ref name="FAA Radar">{{Cite web |date=2020 |title=Airport Surveillance Radar |url=https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/technology/asr-11/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161417/https://www.faa.gov/air_traffic/technology/asr-11 |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=3 September 2022 |website=Air traffic control, technology |publisher=US Federal Aviation Administration website}}</ref>
** [[Secondary surveillance radar]] – Aircraft carry [[Transponder (aeronautics)|radar transponders]], transceivers which when triggered by the incoming radar signal transmit a return microwave signal.  This causes the aircraft to show up more strongly on the radar screen.  The radar which triggers the transponder and receives the return beam, usually mounted on top of the primary radar dish, is called the [[secondary surveillance radar]].  Since radar cannot measure an aircraft's altitude with any accuracy, the transponder also transmits back the aircraft's altitude measured by its [[altimeter]], and an ID number identifying the aircraft, which is displayed on the radar screen.<ref name="Binns">{{Cite book |last=Binns |first=Chris |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N5lxDwAAQBAJ&q=Secondary+surveillance+radar |title=Aircraft Systems: Instruments, Communications, Navigation, and Control |publisher=Wiley |year=2018 |isbn=978-1119259541 |access-date=11 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161258/https://books.google.com/books?id=N5lxDwAAQBAJ&q=Secondary+surveillance+radar#v=snippet&q=Secondary%20surveillance%20radar&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[Electronic countermeasures]] (ECM) – Military defensive electronic systems designed to degrade enemy radar effectiveness, or deceive it with false information, to prevent enemies from locating local forces.  It often consists of powerful microwave transmitters that can mimic enemy radar signals to create false target indications on the enemy radar screens.<ref name="Artech-Horizon House">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Y8kePYFK1L8C&q=Electronic+countermeasures |title=International Electronic Countermeasures Handbook |publisher=Artech/Horizon House |year=2004 |isbn=978-1580538985 |access-date=11 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161259/https://books.google.com/books?id=Y8kePYFK1L8C&q=Electronic+countermeasures#v=snippet&q=Electronic%20countermeasures&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Rotating_marine_radar_-_rotating_waveguide_antenna.gif|thumb|Rotating marine radar antenna on a ship]]

* [[Marine radar]] – an [[S band|S]] or [[X band]] radar on ships used to detect nearby ships and obstructions like bridges.<ref name="Bhattacharjee-2021">{{Cite web |last=Bhattacharjee |first=Shilavadra |date=2021 |title=Marine Radars and Their Use in the Shipping Industry |url=https://www.marineinsight.com/marine-navigation/marine-radars-and-their-use-in-the-shipping-industry/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161408/https://www.marineinsight.com/marine-navigation/marine-radars-and-their-use-in-the-shipping-industry/ |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=3 September 2022 |publisher=Marine Insight website}}</ref>  A rotating antenna sweeps a vertical fan-shaped beam of microwaves around the water surface surrounding the craft out to the horizon.
* [[Weather radar]] – A [[Doppler radar]] which maps weather precipitation intensities and wind speeds with the echoes returned from raindrops and their [[radial velocity]] by their [[Doppler shift]].<ref name="NWS">{{Cite web |date=2020 |title=Using and Understanding Doppler Radar |url=https://www.weather.gov/mkx/using-radar |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161300/https://www.weather.gov/mkx/using-radar |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=3 September 2022 |website=US National Weather Service website |publisher=US National Weather Service, NOAA}}</ref>
* [[Phased-array radar]] – a radar set that uses a [[phased array]], a computer-controlled antenna that can steer the radar beam quickly to point in different directions without moving the antenna.  Phased-array radars were developed by the military to track fast-moving missiles and aircraft.  They are widely used in military equipment and are now spreading to civilian applications.<ref name="Fenn">{{Cite book |last=Fenn |first=Alan J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k1MmAgAAQBAJ&q=Phased-array+radar |title=Adaptive Antennas and Phased Arrays for Radar and Communications |publisher=Artech House |year=2007 |isbn=978-1596932739 |access-date=11 September 2022}}</ref>
* [[Synthetic aperture radar]] (SAR) – a specialized airborne radar set that produces a high-resolution map of ground terrain.  The radar is mounted on an aircraft or spacecraft and the radar antenna radiates a beam of radio waves sideways at right angles to the direction of motion, toward the ground.  In processing the return radar signal, the motion of the vehicle is used to simulate a large antenna, giving the radar a higher resolution.<ref name="Teeuw">{{Cite book |last=Teeuw |first=R.M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Zy-94WdP3dgC&dq=Synthetic+aperture+radar+ground+terrain&pg=PA45 |title=Mapping Hazardous Terrain Using Remote Sensing |publisher=Geological Society of London |year=2007 |isbn=978-1862392298 |access-date=11 September 2022}}</ref>
* [[Ground-penetrating radar]] – a specialized radar instrument that is rolled along the ground surface in a cart and transmits a beam of radio waves into the ground, producing an image of subsurface objects.  Frequencies from 100&nbsp;MHz to a few GHz are used.  Since radio waves cannot penetrate very far into earth, the depth of GPR is limited to about 50 feet.<ref name="Jol">{{Cite book |last=Jol |first=Harry M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y__uIi-5RvgC&q=Ground+Penetrating+Radar+Theory+and+Applications |title=Ground Penetrating Radar Theory and Applications |publisher=Elsevier |year=2008 |isbn=978-0080951843 |access-date=10 September 2022}}</ref>
* [[Collision avoidance system]] – a short range radar or [[LIDAR]] system on an automobile or vehicle that detects if the vehicle is about to collide with an object and applies the brakes to prevent the collision.<ref name="Grosch">{{Cite journal |last=Grosch |first=Theodore O. |date=30 June 1995 |title=Radar sensors for automotive collision warning and avoidance |url=https://www.spiedigitallibrary.org/conference-proceedings-of-spie/2463/0000/Radar-sensors-for-automotive-collision-warning-and-avoidance/10.1117/12.212749.short?SSO=1 |journal=Synthetic Vision for Vehicle Guidance and Control |publisher=Society of Photo-Optical Instrumentation Engineers |volume=2463 |pages=239–247 |bibcode=1995SPIE.2463..239G |doi=10.1117/12.212749 |s2cid=110665898 |url-access=subscription |access-date=10 September 2022 |editor-first1=Jacques G. |editor-last1=Verly}}</ref>
* [[Fuze#Proximity fuze|Radar fuze]] – a [[detonator]] for an [[aerial bomb]] which uses a radar altimeter to measure the height of the bomb above the ground as it falls and detonates it at a certain altitude.<ref name="Brodie-Brodie">{{Cite book |last1=Brodie |first1=Bernard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mAsrwMrfaoQC&dq=radar+fuse+bomb&pg=PA213 |title=From Crossbow to H-bomb |last2=Brodie |first2=Fawn McKay |publisher=Indiana University Press |year=1973 |isbn=0253201616 |access-date=10 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161829/https://books.google.com/books?id=mAsrwMrfaoQC&dq=radar+fuse+bomb&pg=PA213#v=onepage&q=radar%20fuse%20bomb&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Radiolocation ===
{{main|Radiolocation}}

Radiolocation is a generic term covering a variety of techniques that use radio waves to find the location of objects, or for navigation.<ref name="Sharp-Yu">{{Cite book |last1=Sharp |first1=Ian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pHFdDwAAQBAJ&q=Wireless+Positioning%3A+Principles+and+Practice |title=Wireless Positioning: Principles and Practice, Navigation: Science and Technology |last2=Yu |first2=Kegen |publisher=Springer |year=2018 |isbn=978-9811087912 |access-date=10 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161829/https://books.google.com/books?id=pHFdDwAAQBAJ&q=Wireless+Positioning%3A+Principles+and+Practice#v=snippet&q=Wireless%20Positioning%3A%20Principles%20and%20Practice&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
[[File:HA0478-006_(6011470974).jpg|left|thumb|An early [[iPhone]] with its GPS navigation app in use.]]

* [[Global Navigation Satellite System]] (GNSS) or ''satnav system'' – A system of satellites which allows geographical location on Earth ([[latitude]], [[longitude]], and altitude/elevation) to be determined to high precision (within a few metres) by small portable navigation instruments, by timing the arrival of radio signals from the satellites.  These are the most widely used navigation systems today.  The main satellite navigation systems are the US [[Global Positioning System]] (GPS), Russia's [[GLONASS]], China's [[BeiDou Navigation Satellite System]] (BDS) and the [[European Union]]'s [[Galileo (satellite navigation)|Galileo]].<ref name="Teunissen-Montenbruck">{{Cite book |last1=Teunissen |first1=Peter |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=93goDwAAQBAJ&q=Global+Navigation+Satellite+System |title=Springer Handbook of Global Navigation Satellite Systems |last2=Montenbruck |first2=Oliver |publisher=Springer |year=2017 |isbn=978-3319429281 |access-date=10 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161934/https://books.google.com/books?id=93goDwAAQBAJ&q=Global+Navigation+Satellite+System#v=snippet&q=Global%20Navigation%20Satellite%20System&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Paris-PorteMolitor-GPS.jpg|thumb|A ''[[personal navigation assistant]]'' by [[Garmin]], which uses GPS to give driving directions to a destination.]]

** [[Global Positioning System]] (GPS) – The most widely used satellite navigation system, maintained by the US Air Force, which uses a constellation of 31 satellites in [[low Earth orbit]].  The orbits of the satellites are distributed so at any time at least four satellites are above the horizon over each point on Earth.  Each satellite has an onboard [[atomic clock]] and transmits a continuous radio signal containing a precise time signal as well as its current position. Two frequencies are used, 1.2276 and 1.57542&nbsp;GHz. Since the velocity of radio waves is virtually constant, the delay of the radio signal from a satellite is proportional to the distance of the receiver from the satellite.  By receiving the signals from at least four satellites a [[GPS receiver]] can calculate its position on Earth by comparing the arrival time of the radio signals.  Since each satellite's position is known precisely at any given time, from the delay the position of the receiver can be calculated by a microprocessor in the receiver. The position can be displayed as latitude and longitude, or as a marker on an electronic map.  GPS receivers are incorporated in almost all cellphones and in vehicles such as automobiles, aircraft, and ships, and are used to guide [[Unmanned aerial vehicle|drones]], [[missiles]], [[cruise missiles]], and even [[artillery shells]] to their target, and handheld GPS receivers are produced for hikers and the military.<ref name="El-Rabbany">{{Cite book |last=El-Rabbany |first=Ahmed |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=U2JmghrrB8cC&q=how+GPS+works |title=Introduction to GPS: The Global Positioning System |publisher=Artech House |year=2002 |isbn=978-1580531832 |access-date=10 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161831/https://books.google.com/books?id=U2JmghrrB8cC&q=how+GPS+works#v=snippet&q=how%20GPS%20works&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Kiland-Silverstein Gray">{{Cite book |last1=Kiland |first1=Taylor Baldwin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAhiDwAAQBAJ&q=how+GPS+works+military |title=The Military GPS: Cutting Edge Global Positioning System |last2=Silverstein Gray |first2=Judy |date=15 July 2016 |publisher=Enslow Publishing |isbn=978-0766075184 |access-date=10 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161833/https://books.google.com/books?id=uAhiDwAAQBAJ&q=how+GPS+works+military#v=snippet&q=how%20GPS%20works%20military&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[Radio beacon]] – a fixed location terrestrial radio transmitter which transmits a continuous radio signal used by aircraft and ships for [[navigation]].  The locations of beacons are plotted on navigational maps used by aircraft and ships.<ref name="Deltour">{{Cite web |last=Deltour |first=B.V. |date=August 1960 |title=A Guide To Nav-Com Equipment |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QETktYruMwsC&dq=radio+beacon+continuous+radio+signal&pg=PA44 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161833/https://books.google.com/books?id=QETktYruMwsC&dq=radio+beacon+continuous+radio+signal&pg=PA44#v=onepage&q=radio%20beacon%20continuous%20radio%20signal&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=10 September 2022 |publisher=Flying Magazine Aug 1960}}</ref>

[[File:D-VOR_PEK.JPG|thumb|VOR antenna, Beijing]]

:* [[VHF omnidirectional range]] (VOR) – a worldwide aircraft [[radio navigation]] system consisting of fixed ground [[radio beacons]] transmitting between 108.00 and 117.95&nbsp;MHz in the [[very high frequency]] (VHF) band.<ref name="FAA2">{{cite web |date=4 December 2023 |title=Very High Frequency Omnidirectional Range |url=https://www.faa.gov/about/office_org/headquarters_offices/ato/service_units/techops/navservices/gbng/vor |accessdate=25 October 2024 |work=Navigation services |publisher=US Federal Aviation Administration website, US Dept. of Commerce |format= |doi=}}</ref><ref name="Helfrick2">{{cite book |last=Helfrick |first=Albert |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0BI6ioB8kM8C&pg=PA27 |title=Principles of Avionics |date=2010 |publisher=Avionics Communications |isbn=978-1-885544-27-8 |location= |pages=27 |language= |doi= |jfm= |mr= |zbl= |id=}}</ref>  An automated navigational instrument on the aircraft displays a [[Bearing (navigation)|bearing]] to a nearby VOR transmitter. A VOR beacon transmits two signals simultaneously on different frequencies.  A [[directional antenna]] transmits a beam of radio waves that rotates like a lighthouse at a fixed rate, 30 times per second. When the directional beam is facing north, an [[omnidirectional antenna]] transmits a pulse. By measuring the difference in [[Phase (waves)|phase]] of these two signals, an aircraft can determine its [[Bearing (navigation)|bearing]] (or "radial") from the station accurately. By taking a bearing on two VOR beacons an aircraft can determine its position (called a "fix") to an accuracy of about {{convert|90|m|ft|sigfig=2}}.  Most VOR beacons also have a distance measuring capability, called [[distance measuring equipment]] (DME); these are called VOR/DME's.  The aircraft transmits a radio signal to the VOR/DME beacon and a [[transponder]] transmits a return signal.  From the [[propagation delay]] between the transmitted and received signal the aircraft can calculate its distance from the beacon.  This allows an aircraft to determine its location "fix" from only one VOR beacon.  Since line-of-sight VHF frequencies are used VOR beacons have a range of about 200 miles for aircraft at cruising altitude. [[TACAN]] is a similar military radio beacon system which transmits in 962–1213&nbsp;MHz, and a combined VOR and TACAN beacon is called a [[VORTAC]]. The number of VOR beacons is declining as aviation switches to the [[RNAV]] system that relies on [[Global Positioning System]] satellite navigation.<ref name="USDOD">{{Cite web |year=2009 |title=2008 Federal Radionavigation Plan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x5sRi3P-B-EC&q=2008+Federal+Radionavigation+Plan |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003161834/https://books.google.com/books?id=x5sRi3P-B-EC&q=2008+Federal+Radionavigation+Plan#v=snippet&q=2008%20Federal%20Radionavigation%20Plan&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=10 September 2022 |publisher=U.S. Department of Defense}}</ref><ref name="Martin">{{Cite web |last=Martin |first=Swayne |title=How A VOR Works |url=https://www.boldmethod.com/learn-to-fly/navigation/how-a-vor-works/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162345/https://www.boldmethod.com/learn-to-fly/navigation/how-a-vor-works/ |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=10 September 2022 |website=boldmethod.com |publisher=Boldmethod -Digital Aviation Content}}</ref>

[[File:London_Heathrow_Instrument_Landing_System_(ILS),_October_2023_03.jpg|thumb|Localizer antenna array at Heathrow Airport, London]]

:* [[Instrument Landing System]] (ILS) - A short range radio navigation aid at [[airports]] which guides aircraft landing in low visibility conditions.  It consists of multiple antennas at the end of each [[runway]] that radiate two beams of radio waves along the approach to the runway: the ''[[localizer]]'' (108 to 111.95&nbsp;MHz frequency), which provides horizontal guidance, a heading line to keep the aircraft centered on the runway, and the ''[[glideslope]]'' (329.15 to 335&nbsp;MHz) for vertical guidance, to keep the aircraft descending at the proper rate for a smooth touchdown at the correct point on the runway.  Each aircraft has a receiver instrument and antenna which receives the beams, with an indicator to tell the pilot whether he is on the correct horizontal and vertical approach. The ILS beams are receivable for at least 15 miles, and have a radiated power of 25 watts.  ILS systems at airports are being replaced by systems that use satellite navigation.<ref name="FAA Airports">{{cite web |date=4 December 2023 |title=Instrument Landing System |url=https://www.faa.gov/about/office_org/headquarters_offices/ato/service_units/techops/navservices/gbng/ils |accessdate=25 October 2024 |work=Navigation services |publisher=US Federal Aviation Administration website, US Dept. of Commerce |format= |doi=}}</ref><ref name="Helfrick">{{cite book |last=Helfrick |first=Albert |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0BI6ioB8kM8C&dq=instrument+landing+system&pg=PA86 |title=Principles of Avionics |date=2010 |publisher=Avionics Communications |isbn=978-1-885544-27-8 |location= |pages=86 |language= |doi= |jfm= |mr= |zbl= |id=}}</ref>
:* [[Non-directional beacon]] (NDB) – Legacy fixed radio beacons used before the VOR system that transmit a simple signal in all directions for aircraft or ships to use for [[radio direction finding]].  Aircraft use [[automatic direction finder]] (ADF) receivers which use a [[directional antenna]] to determine the [[Bearing (navigation)|bearing]] to the beacon.  By taking bearings on two beacons they can determine their position.  NDBs use frequencies between 190 and 1750&nbsp;kHz in the [[Low frequency|LF]] and [[Medium frequency|MF]] bands which propagate beyond the horizon as [[Ground wave|ground waves]] or [[skywaves]] much farther than VOR beacons.  They transmit a [[callsign]] consisting of one to 3 [[Morse code]] letters as an identifier.<ref name="SI">{{Cite web |title=Non-Directional Beacon (NDB) |url=https://www.systemsinterface.com/products/navaids/ndb/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162349/https://www.systemsinterface.com/solutions/navigation/ndb |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=10 September 2022 |website=systemsinterface.com |publisher=Systems Interface}}</ref>

[[File:EPIRB_(1).jpg|thumb|EPIRB emergency locator beacon on a ship]]

* [[Emergency locator beacon]] – a portable battery powered [[radio transmitter]] used in emergencies to locate airplanes, vessels, and persons in distress and in need of immediate rescue.  Various types of emergency locator beacons are carried by aircraft, ships, vehicles, hikers and cross-country skiers.  In the event of an emergency, such as the aircraft crashing, the ship sinking, or a hiker becoming lost, the transmitter is deployed and begins to transmit a continuous radio signal, which is used by [[search and rescue]] teams to quickly find the emergency and render aid.  The latest generation [[Emergency Position Indicating Rescue Beacon|Emergency Position Indicating Rescue Beacons]] (EPIRBs) contain a [[GPS receiver]], and broadcast to rescue teams their exact location within 20 meters.<ref name="CBC">{{Cite web |title=How does an emergency beacon work? |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/science/how-does-an-emergency-beacon-work-1.1327070 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162348/https://www.cbc.ca/news/science/how-does-an-emergency-beacon-work-1.1327070 |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=10 September 2022 |website=cbc.ca |publisher=CBC News}}</ref>
** [[Cospas-Sarsat]] – an international humanitarian consortium of governmental and private agencies which acts as a dispatcher for [[search and rescue]] operations.  It operates a network of around 65 [[satellites]] carrying radio receivers, which detect distress signals from [[Emergency locator beacon|emergency locator beacons]] anywhere on Earth transmitting on the international Cospas distress frequency of 406&nbsp;MHz.  The satellites calculate the geographic location of the beacon within 2&nbsp;km by measuring the [[Doppler shift|Doppler frequency shift]] of the radio waves due to the relative motion of the transmitter and the satellite, and quickly transmit the information to the appropriate local [[first responder]] organizations, which perform the [[search and rescue]].<ref name="cospas-sarsat">{{Cite web |title=What is a Cospas-Sarsat Beacon? |url=http://www.cospas-sarsat.int/en/18-frontpage-articles/603-what-is-a-cospas-sarsat-beacon |access-date=10 September 2022 |website=cospas-sarsat.int |publisher=International Cospas-Sarsat Programme}}</ref><ref name="NASA1985">{{Cite web |year=1985 |title=Scientific and Technical Aerospace Reports, Volume 23, Issue 20 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wg50RfqjLWMC&dq=cospas-sarsat.int+2km&pg=PA3400 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162347/https://books.google.com/books?id=wg50RfqjLWMC&dq=cospas-sarsat.int+2km&pg=PA3400#v=onepage&q=cospas-sarsat.int%202km&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=10 September 2022 |publisher=NASA, Office of Scientific and Technical Information}}</ref>

[[File:Tracking_Mountain_Lions.jpg|thumb|Wildlife officer tracking radio-tagged mountain lion]]

* [[Radio direction finding]] (RDF) – this is a general technique, used since the early 1900s, of using specialized radio receivers with [[Directional antenna|directional antennas]] (RDF receivers) to determine the exact [[Bearing (navigation)|bearing]] of a radio signal, to determine the location of the transmitter.  The location of a terrestrial transmitter can be determined by simple [[triangulation]] from bearings taken by two RDF stations separated geographically, as the point where the two bearing lines cross, this is called a "fix".  Military forces use RDF to locate enemy forces by their tactical radio transmissions, [[counterintelligence]] services use it to locate clandestine transmitters used by [[Espionage|espionage agents]], and governments use it to locate unlicensed transmitters or interference sources.  Older RDF receivers used rotatable [[loop antennas]], the antenna is rotated until the radio signal strength is weakest, indicating the transmitter is in one of the antenna's two [[Null (radio)|nulls]].  The nulls are used since they are sharper than the antenna's [[Main lobe|lobes]] (maxima).  More modern receivers use [[phased array]] antennas which have a much greater angular resolution.<ref name="defenceweb">{{Cite web |date=8 January 2021 |title=An Introduction to Radio Direction Finding |url=https://www.defenceweb.co.za/virtual-press-offices/111485/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162351/https://www.defenceweb.co.za/virtual-press-offices/111485/ |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=10 September 2022 |website=defenceweb.co.za |publisher=defenceWeb}}</ref><ref name="Moell-Curlee">{{Cite book |last1=Moell |first1=Joseph D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RfzF2-fHJ6MC&q=Radio+direction+finding |title=Transmitter Hunting: Radio Direction Finding Simplified |last2=Curlee |first2=Thomas N. |publisher=McGraw Hill Professional |year=1987 |isbn=978-0830627011 |access-date=10 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162348/https://books.google.com/books?id=RfzF2-fHJ6MC&q=Radio+direction+finding |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
** [[Animal migration tracking]] – a widely used technique in [[wildlife biology]], [[conservation biology]], and [[wildlife management]] in which small battery-powered radio transmitters are attached to [[wild animals]] so their movements can be tracked with a directional [[Radio direction finding|RDF]] receiver. Sometimes the transmitter is implanted in the animal.  The VHF band is typically used since antennas in this band are fairly compact.  The receiver has a [[directional antenna]] (typically a small [[Yagi antenna|Yagi]]) which is rotated until the received signal is strongest; at this point the antenna is pointing in the direction of the animal.  Sophisticated systems used in recent years use satellites to track the animal, or [[geolocation]] tags with [[GPS]] receivers which record and transmit a log of the animal's location.<ref name="Smithsonian">{{Cite web |title=Radio telemetry |url=http://migratoryconnectivityproject.org/vhf-radios/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220910191603/http://migratoryconnectivityproject.org/vhf-radios/ |archive-date=10 September 2022 |access-date=10 September 2022 |publisher=Migratory Connectivity Project, Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center}}</ref>

=== Remote control ===
{{main|Radio control}}
[[File:MQ-1_Predator_unmanned_aircraft.jpg|thumb|US Air Force [[MQ-1 Predator]] drone flown remotely by a pilot on the ground]]
Radio remote control is the use of electronic [[Control signal|control signals]] sent by radio waves from a transmitter to control the actions of a device at a remote location.  Remote control systems may also include telemetry channels in the other direction, used to transmit real-time information on the state of the device back to the control station. Uncrewed [[spacecraft]] are an example of remote-controlled machines, controlled by commands transmitted by [[Satellite ground station|satellite ground stations]].  Most handheld [[remote controls]] used to control [[consumer electronics]] products like televisions or DVD players actually operate by [[infrared light]] rather than radio waves, so are not examples of radio remote control.  A security concern with remote control systems is [[Spoofing attack|spoofing]], in which an unauthorized person transmits an imitation of the control signal to take control of the device.<ref name="Layton">{{Cite web |last=Layton |first=Julia |date=10 November 2005 |title=How Remote Controls Work |url=https://electronics.howstuffworks.com/remote-control3.htm |access-date=10 September 2022 |publisher=HowStuff Works}}</ref>  Examples of radio remote control:

* [[Unmanned aerial vehicle]] (UAV, drone) – A drone is an aircraft without an onboard pilot, flown by remote control by a pilot in another location, usually in a piloting station on the ground.  They are used by the military for reconnaissance and ground attack, and more recently by the civilian world for news reporting and [[aerial photography]].  The pilot uses aircraft controls like a joystick or steering wheel, which create control signals which are transmitted to the drone by radio to control the flight surfaces and engine.  A telemetry system transmits back a video image from a camera in the drone to allow the pilot to see where the aircraft is going, and data from a [[GPS receiver]] giving the real-time position of the aircraft.  UAVs have sophisticated onboard [[automatic pilot]] systems that maintain stable flight and only require manual control to change directions.<ref name="Sadraey">{{Cite book |last=Sadraey |first=Mohammad H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zlbSDwAAQBAJ&dq=UAV+telemetry&pg=PA535 |title=Design of Unmanned Aerial Systems |publisher=Wiley |year=2020 |isbn=978-1119508694 |access-date=10 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162350/https://books.google.com/books?id=zlbSDwAAQBAJ&dq=UAV+telemetry&pg=PA535#v=onepage&q=UAV%20telemetry&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Automobile_remote_keyless_entry_transmitter.jpg|thumb|Remote keyless entry fob for a car]]

* [[Keyless entry system]] – a short-range handheld battery powered [[key fob]] transmitter, included with most modern cars, which can lock and unlock the doors of a vehicle from outside, eliminating the need to use a key.  When a button is pressed, the transmitter sends a coded radio signal to a receiver in the vehicle, operating the locks.  The fob must be close to the vehicle, typically within 5 to 20 meters.  North America and Japan use a frequency of 315&nbsp;MHz, while Europe uses 433.92 and 868&nbsp;MHz.  Some models can also remotely start the engine, to warm up the car.  A security concern with all keyless entry systems is a [[replay attack]], in which a thief uses a special receiver ("code grabber") to record the radio signal during opening, which can later be replayed to open the door.  To prevent this, keyless systems use a [[rolling code]] system in which a [[pseudorandom number generator]] in the remote control generates a different random key each time it is used.  To prevent thieves from simulating the pseudorandom generator to calculate the next key, the radio signal is also [[encrypted]].<ref name="Smith">{{Cite book |last=Smith |first=Craig |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vAYvDwAAQBAJ&dq=keyless+entry+system+315+MHz&pg=PA216 |title=The Car Hacker's Handbook: A Guide for the Penetration Tester |date=2016 |publisher=No Starch Press |isbn=978-1593277703 |access-date=10 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162351/https://books.google.com/books?id=vAYvDwAAQBAJ&dq=keyless+entry+system+315+MHz&pg=PA216#v=onepage&q=keyless%20entry%20system%20315%20MHz&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
** [[Garage door opener]] – a short-range handheld transmitter which can open or close a building's electrically operated [[garage door]] from outside, so the owner can open the door upon arrival, and close it after departure.  When a button is pressed the control transmits a coded [[Frequency-shift keying|FSK]] radio signal to a receiver in the opener, raising or lowering the door.  Modern openers use 310, 315 or 390&nbsp;MHz.  To prevent a thief using a [[replay attack]], modern openers use a [[rolling code]] system.<ref name="Pinkerton">{{Cite book |last=Pinkerton |first=Alasdair |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cRieDwAAQBAJ&dq=Garage+door+opener++390+mhz&pg=PT24 |title=Radio: Making Waves in Sound |date=15 June 2019 |publisher=Reaktion Books |isbn=978-1789140996 |access-date=9 September 2022}}</ref><ref name="Biffl-Eckhart-Luder-Weippl">{{Cite book |last1=Biffl |first1=Stefan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c1S9DwAAQBAJ&dq=Garage+door+opener++replay+attack&pg=PA435 |title=Security and Quality in Cyber-Physical Systems Engineering |last2=Eckhart |first2=Matthias |last3=Lüder |first3=Arndt |last4=Weippl |first4=Edgar |publisher=Springer Nature |year=2019 |isbn=978-3030253127 |access-date=9 September 2022}}</ref>

[[File:Md4-200.jpg|thumb|[[Quadcopter]], a popular remote-controlled toy]]

* [[Radio-controlled models]] – a popular hobby is playing with radio-controlled model boats, cars, airplanes, and helicopters ([[quadcopters]]) which are controlled by radio signals from a handheld console with a [[joystick]].  Most recent transmitters use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz [[ISM band]] with multiple control channels modulated with [[Pulse-width modulation|PWM]], [[PCM]] or FSK.<ref name="Boukerche">{{Cite book |last=Boukerche |first=Azzedine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bI05X9-4tw8C&dq=radio+controlled+models+2.4+ghz+ism&pg=PA46 |title=Algorithms and Protocols for Wireless and Mobile Ad Hoc Networks |publisher=Wiley |year=2008 |isbn=978-0470396377 |access-date=9 September 2022}}</ref>
* [[Doorbell|Wireless doorbell]] – A residential [[doorbell]] that uses wireless technology to eliminate the need to run wires through the building walls.  It consists of a doorbell button beside the door containing a small battery powered transmitter.  When the doorbell is pressed it sends a signal to a receiver inside the house with a speaker that sounds chimes to indicate someone is at the door.  They usually use the 2.4&nbsp;GHz ISM band.  The frequency channel used can usually be changed by the owner in case another nearby doorbell is using the same channel.<ref name="Wonning">{{Cite web |last=Wonning |first=Paul R. |date=12 May 2021 |title=A Guide to the Home Electric System |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=INctEAAAQBAJ&dq=wireless+doorbell&pg=PT34 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162922/https://books.google.com/books?id=INctEAAAQBAJ&dq=wireless+doorbell&pg=PT34#v=onepage&q=wireless%20doorbell&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |access-date=9 September 2022 |publisher=Mossy Feet Books}}</ref><ref name="Chatterjee-Kumar-Jain-Rathore">{{Cite book |last1=Chatterjee |first1=Jyotir Moy |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-9MWEAAAQBAJ&dq=wireless+doorbells+2.4+ghz+ism&pg=PR7 |title=Internet of Things and Machine Learning in Agriculture: Technological Impacts and Challenges |last2=Kumar |first2=Abhishek |last3=Jain |first3=Vishal |last4=Rathore |first4=Pramod Singh |publisher=Walter de Gruyter GmbH & Co KG |year=2021 |isbn=978-3110691283 |access-date=9 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162920/https://books.google.com/books?id=-9MWEAAAQBAJ&dq=wireless+doorbells+2.4+ghz+ism&pg=PR7#v=onepage&q=wireless%20doorbells%202.4%20ghz%20ism&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Scientific research ===

* [[Radio astronomy]] is the scientific study of radio waves emitted by astronomical objects.  Radio astronomers use [[radio telescopes]], large radio antennas and receivers, to receive and study the radio waves from [[Astronomical radio source|astronomical radio sources]].  Since astronomical radio sources are so far away, the radio waves from them are extremely weak, requiring extremely sensitive receivers, and radio telescopes are the most sensitive radio receivers in existence.  They use large [[Parabolic antenna|parabolic (dish) antennas]] up to {{convert|500|meters|feet|sigfig=1}} in diameter to collect enough radio wave energy to study.  The [[RF front end]] electronics of the receiver is often cooled by [[liquid nitrogen]] to reduce [[thermal noise]].  Multiple antennas are often linked together in arrays which function as a single antenna, to increase collecting power.  In [[Very Long Baseline Interferometry]] (VLBI) radio telescopes on different continents are linked, which can achieve the resolution of an antenna thousands of miles in diameter.<ref name="Yeap-Hirisawa">{{Cite book |last1=Yeap |first1=Kim Ho |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VwfYDwAAQBAJ&q=Analyzing+the+Physics+of+Radio+Telescopes+and+Radio+Astronomy |title=Analyzing the Physics of Radio Telescopes and Radio Astronomy |last2=Hirasawa |first2=Kazuhiro |publisher=IG Global |year=2020 |isbn=978-1799823834 |access-date=9 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162923/https://books.google.com/books?id=VwfYDwAAQBAJ&q=Analyzing+the+Physics+of+Radio+Telescopes+and+Radio+Astronomy#v=snippet&q=Analyzing%20the%20Physics%20of%20Radio%20Telescopes%20and%20Radio%20Astronomy&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Joardar-Clayomb">{{Cite book |last1=Joardar |first1=Shubhendu |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cjW_DgAAQBAJ&q=Radio+Astronomy%3A+An+Introduction |title=Radio Astronomy: An Introduction |last2=Claycomb |first2=J. R. |publisher=Mercury Learning and Information |year=2015 |isbn=978-1937585624 |access-date=2022-09-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162927/https://books.google.com/books?id=cjW_DgAAQBAJ&q=Radio+Astronomy%3A+An+Introduction#v=snippet&q=Radio%20Astronomy%3A%20An%20Introduction&f=false |archive-date=2024-10-03 |url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[Remote sensing]] – in radio, remote sensing is the reception of electromagnetic waves radiated by natural objects or the atmosphere for scientific research.  All warm objects emit [[microwaves]] and the spectrum emitted can be used to determine temperature. [[Microwave radiometer|Microwave radiometers]] are used in [[meteorology]] and [[earth sciences]] to determine temperature of the atmosphere and earth surface, as well as chemical reactions in the atmosphere.<ref name="Chapman-Gasparovic">{{Cite book |last1=Chapman |first1=Rick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=B8Z6EAAAQBAJ&q=Remote+Sensing+Physics%3A+An+Introduction+to+Observing+Earth+from+Space |title=Remote Sensing Physics: An Introduction to Observing Earth from Space |last2=Gasparovic |first2=Richard |publisher=Wiley |year=2022 |isbn=978-1119669074 |access-date=9 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003162924/https://books.google.com/books?id=B8Z6EAAAQBAJ&q=Remote+Sensing+Physics%3A+An+Introduction+to+Observing+Earth+from+Space#v=snippet&q=Remote%20Sensing%20Physics%3A%20An%20Introduction%20to%20Observing%20Earth%20from%20Space&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Pampaloni-Paloscia">{{Cite book |last1=Pampaloni |first1=Paulo |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IwIIhhMxcJwC&q=Remote+Sensing+radiometer |title=Microwave Radiometry and Remote Sensing of the Earth's Surface and Atmosphere |last2=Paloscia |first2=S. |year=2000 |isbn=9067643181 |access-date=9 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003163037/https://books.google.com/books?id=IwIIhhMxcJwC&q=Remote+Sensing+radiometer#v=snippet&q=Remote%20Sensing%20radiometer&f=false |archive-date=3 October 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>
** ''[[Measuring receiver]]'' - a calibrated, laboratory grade radio receiver used to measure the characteristics of radio signals. Often incorporates a [[spectrum analyzer]].
